    Jerry Carl
    Alabama · 1st District
    Committee Assignments
    Not currently serving in Congress.
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Alabama’s 1st District and a former member of Congress, seeking to reclaim the seat he held from January 2021 to January 2025. He lost it in the 2024 Republican primary to Barry Moore, 52–48, after redistricting placed the two incumbents in the same district; the seat is open again in 2026 because Moore is running for the United States Senate. Previously served two terms on the Mobile County Commission (2012–2020), unseating a long-time incumbent in the 2012 primary at 54 and serving as commission president in 2015–2016 and 2019–2020; he declined a taxpayer-funded salary in his first two years. Graduated Sylacauga High School, 1977; attended Lake City Community College in Florida, now Florida Gateway College, intending a career in forestry. No military service; his son’s enlistment in the Marines is what first prompted his interest in public office. Worked briefly at Alabama Power, then started his first business at 25 and went on to found dozens of companies, chiefly in home medical equipment and specialty pharmacy — among them Stat Medical, which he grew to seven locations before selling it to Rotech Medical — along with ventures in real estate, timber and furniture. In Congress he served on the Armed Services and Appropriations committees, working on Alabama’s defense installations including Austal Shipyard in Mobile, Fort Rucker and Redstone Arsenal. Born in Mobile, one of four children raised by a single mother; he and his wife Tina have been married since 1981 and have two children and two grandchildren.

    Rhett Marques
    Alabama · 2nd District
    Committee Assignments
    Not currently serving in Congress.
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Alabama’s 2nd District, challenging Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures, who won the seat in 2024 after a court-ordered redraw created a second majority-Black district in Alabama. Marques won the August 11, 2026 winner-take-all special primary with about 50% against five other candidates, well clear of the runner-up at 20%, with President Trump’s endorsement; he thanked Trump and Senator Katie Britt in his victory speech. He had originally entered the race in the neighboring 1st District in August 2025 before switching. Currently serves in the Alabama House of Representatives for District 91, elected in 2018 and re-elected in 2022, where he is Vice Chair of the Commerce and Small Business Committee and sits on the Health and the Transportation, Utilities and Infrastructure committees; he voted for the 2019 Rebuild Alabama Act raising the state fuel tax. Graduated Fairhope High School, 1990; BS in marketing, University of Alabama, 1994. No military service. Owned and ran Goodson Tire & Auto in Enterprise for more than 26 years, selling the business in 2023 and staying on with the buyer, Jim Whaley Tires. Endorsed by the Alabama AGC PAC. Born in Spanish Fort near Mobile; he met his wife Christina at the University of Alabama, they have been married more than thirty years, and they raised two daughters in Enterprise, in the Wiregrass.     Biography
    Incumbent representing Alabama’s 3rd District since 2003, succeeding Bob Riley. Previously served on the Calhoun County Commission (1987–1991), elected at 28 as its youngest member and first Republican, and in the Alabama House of Representatives (1994–2002), where he was House Minority Leader from 1998. Graduated Saks High School, Anniston; BA in political science, Jacksonville State University, 1981; MPA, Jacksonville State University, 1984; JD, Birmingham School of Law, 1991, with honors. No military service; his father was a firefighter at Anniston Army Depot and his mother a textile worker. He and his wife Beth worked their way through law school at night; he then ran a general law practice in Anniston, later his own firm, and has been a small business owner. Worked for the United Way in Calhoun County while on the commission. Chairman of the Armed Services Committee since January 2023, having been its ranking member from 2021, and ranking member of Homeland Security from 2019 to 2021. Named Anniston Star Citizen of the Year in 1998. A sixth-generation East Alabamian, born in Hammond, Indiana, and raised in the mill village of Blue Mountain.

    Incumbent representing Alabama’s 4th District since January 1997, succeeding Tom Bevill and sworn in for a fifteenth term on January 7, 2025. No military service; an only child, the son of a circuit judge of more than 30 years who was also a part-time minister to a small group of Congregational churches in northwest Alabama. Practiced law privately in Haleyville for about two years before taking the bench. Chairman of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, Education and Related Agencies — responsible for the largest non-defense portion of the federal budget — and also serves on its Agriculture and Defense subcommittees. Chairs the Values Action Team. Secured $100 million in 2000 for the Corridor X highway plan between Birmingham and Memphis, and has backed loan guarantees for domestic steel, drawing AFL-CIO support. Holds Trump’s endorsement for 2026. Lives in Haleyville.

    Biography
    Incumbent representing Alabama’s 5th District since January 2023, succeeding Mo Brooks. Previously served on the Madison County Commission for the 4th District from 1996, elected at 26 as the youngest Republican officeholder in Alabama at the time, and as the commission’s first Republican chairman from 2012 to 2023. Graduated Sparkman High School, 1988; BS in business administration, Athens State University; EMT license, University of Alabama in Huntsville. No military service. Began volunteering at the Monrovia Fire-Rescue Department at 13, which his father Horace helped found, and served for years as a volunteer firefighter, EMT and 911 dispatcher; awarded the state Public Safety Officer Medal of Honor for his service after the November 1989 Huntsville tornado. Grew up working in his father’s country store and helped build the family charter bus business to eight coaches, which put him and his siblings through college; later worked in public relations for First Alabama Bank and as a sales representative for Solvay Pharmaceuticals. As commission chairman he led the clean-up after the April 2011 tornado outbreak, in which more than 350 homes in the area were destroyed and nine people died, and worked to recruit Toyota Mazda, Polaris, Blue Origin and GE Aviation to North Alabama. Chairman of the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Emergency Management and Technology and Vice Chair of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies. His district takes in Huntsville and Redstone Arsenal.

    Biography
    Incumbent representing Alabama’s 6th District since January 2015, succeeding Spencer Bachus. No prior elected office; appointed to Governor Fob James’s Welfare Reform Commission, Governor Bob Riley’s Task Force to Strengthen Alabama Families, and Governor Robert Bentley’s Commission on Improving State Government. Graduated Hackleburg High School, 1972; attended Northwest Alabama Junior College (1972–1974); BS in operations management, University of Alabama, 1977, where he was the first person on either side of his family to attend college and a walk-on member of the football team under Paul “Bear” Bryant. No military service. Worked twelve years in the private sector, nine of them with two major international engineering and construction companies, before involvement with Focus on the Family led him to co-found the Alabama Family Alliance in 1989; it was renamed the Alabama Policy Institute in 2000 and he served as its president for some 24 years, stepping down to run for Congress in 2014. A founding board member of the State Policy Network in 1992, serving six years on its board, the last two as chairman. Chairman of the House Republican Policy Committee from 2019 to 2025, succeeded by Kevin Hern, and previously chaired the Oversight Subcommittee on Intergovernmental Affairs. Chairman of the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment since the committee’s July 2025 reshuffle, having previously chaired its Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee. Born in Haleyville and raised in Hackleburg, one of four children; his father was a logger without a high school education and his mother trained as a nurse while he was in college. Lives in Hoover.

    Ammie Akin
    Alabama · 7th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Alabama’s 7th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Terri Sewell, who is seeking a ninth consecutive term and faced no primary opponent. Akin won the August 11, 2026 special Republican primary with 72.6% — 6,094 votes to retired pastor David Perry’s 2,302 — on 5.24% turnout. The primary was one of four Alabama held that day: after a special legislative session, Governor Kay Ivey called special elections in the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th districts once a United States Supreme Court order allowed the state to use the congressional map the Legislature passed in 2023 rather than the court-ordered one. That 2023 map had previously been struck down as racially discriminatory, and the court-drawn map used in 2024 produced the election of two Black representatives, a first in Alabama history. Republicans reshaped the 2nd District to make it more likely to elect a Republican, and the new map altered three other districts including Sewell’s. The 7th covers west-central Alabama including parts of Jefferson and Tuscaloosa counties and has not been represented by a Republican in more than six decades. No prior elected office. A longtime educator in the Birmingham area: she served as an assistant superintendent in a public school system and as interim superintendent of a private Christian school, and founded a nonprofit. On the redistricting turmoil she has said she would rather not discuss what is outside her control, arguing the district’s people “deserve representation... deserve to be noticed, they deserve to be heard.”
    NOTE: Alabama used special primaries on Aug 11, 2026 under a 2023 congressional map cleared by the Supreme Court in June - district lines differ from the map used in 2024.

    Biography
    Incumbent representing Alaska At-Large since 2025. No prior elected office. BBA in entrepreneurship, Baylor University, 1999; MBA, Indiana University–Bloomington, 2002. No military service. Worked at Ford Motor Company in technology, finance and product development before returning to Alaska in 2004; founded FarShore Partners, a technology development company, and co-founded Dashfire, a startup investor. Co-chaired the Alaska Republican Party’s Finance Committee and Rep. Don Young’s 2020 re-election campaign, and served on the board of Alaska Policy Forum. Six of his bills have been signed into law since January 2025, more than any other member of the 119th Congress; Speaker Mike Johnson called him an historically effective member and campaigned with him in Alaska. A Freedom Caucus member who holds Trump’s endorsement, given unusually early in May 2025. Vice Chair of the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines and Hazardous Materials; also sits on Science, Space and Technology. His grandfather Nick Begich Sr. held this same seat as a Democrat; his uncles are former Sen. Mark Begich and Tom Begich. Led the August 18, 2026 top-four primary with 46.7%, ahead of independent Bill Hill at 30.9%; Democrat Matt Schultz suspended his campaign and endorsed Hill too late to leave the ballot, finishing third at 8.1%. Alaska has no party nominees: all candidates share one ballot, the top four advance regardless of party, and the November general is decided by ranked-choice voting, so the seat will not be settled by a simple plurality on election night.     Jay Feely
    Arizona · 1st District
    DCCC target
    Biography
    Won the July 21, 2026 Republican primary with 49.8%, beating former state Rep. Joseph Chaplik and businessman John Trobough; AP-projected. Former NFL kicker (14 seasons, six teams including the Arizona Cardinals) and CBS broadcaster; served on a Gilbert school board 2016–2020. Trump gave him a “complete and total endorsement” late in the race. Open seat: Rep. David Schweikert left to run for governor and lost that primary to Andy Biggs. Faces Democrat Amish Shah, a former state representative and physician who narrowly lost to Schweikert in 2024 and beat Marlene Galan-Woods by about 6 points. Note: Feely was criticized for living outside the district — he resides in Biggs’ 5th and originally ran there before Trump endorsed a rival. This Scottsdale-based seat is a competitive open race. Legal name Thomas Feely; born about 1976, a longtime East Valley resident living in Gilbert. Attended the University of Michigan, where he kicked for the 1997 national champion team, and went undrafted in 1999. No military service. Played 14 NFL seasons for seven teams after starting in the Arena Football League — the Atlanta Falcons, New York Giants, Miami Dolphins, Kansas City Chiefs, New York Jets, Arizona Cardinals and Chicago Bears — converting 82.6% of his field goals with a long of 61 yards, and retired after the 2014 season. Served on the NFL Players Association Executive Committee, negotiating with management on behalf of players. Spent the following decade as an NFL analyst for CBS Sports, leaving the booth to run. Founded the Feely Family Foundation with his wife Rebecca to support youth and education, and has worked with Mission of Hope and the Muscular Dystrophy Association. He first launched in the 5th District in April 2025 after Andy Biggs left it, then switched to the 1st in the autumn once Trump endorsed Mark Lamb in the 5th and Schweikert vacated this seat. He has said Trump and Rep. Jim Jordan asked him to run in 2022 but he declined while his children were still in high school, and that the July 2024 assassination attempt on Trump prompted him to reconsider.     Nicholas Glenn
    Arizona · 3rd District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Arizona’s 3rd District, challenging first-term Democratic Rep. Yassamin Ansari. He reached the general as a WRITE-IN candidate in the July 21, 2026 Republican primary, meaning no Republican filed conventionally for the seat. The district covers most of southern, western and downtown Phoenix plus part of Glendale; it is 62.6% Hispanic and rated D+22, and was previously held by Ruben Gallego before he moved to the Senate. Green Party write-in David Redkey and Alan Aversa of the No Labels line are also on the November ballot. A repeat candidate: he ran in this district’s 2024 Republican primary, finishing behind Jeffrey Zink and Jesus Mendoza, and previously ran in Arizona’s 2020 United States Senate contest. No elected office held. A veteran of both the United States Marine Corps and the United States Navy. Works as an engineering technician. Ansari, elected in 2024 to succeed Gallego, was the youngest person ever elected to the Phoenix City Council and the first Iranian American elected to public office in Arizona; educated at Stanford and Cambridge, she has drawn attention in her freshman term as an outspoken critic of the Justice Department’s handling of documents relating to Jeffrey Epstein and has called for the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Little further public record is available on Glenn’s education or platform.

    Zuhdi Jasser
    Arizona · 4th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Arizona’s 4th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Greg Stanton, the former Mayor of Phoenix; the district takes in parts of Tempe, Mesa, Chandler and Ahwatukee Foothills and is competitive by registration, roughly 32% Republican, 30% Democratic and 38% independent. He ran for this seat before, in 2022 and 2024. No prior elected office. Born Mohamed Zuhdi Jasser in Canton, Ohio, on November 17, 1967, a year after his parents fled increasingly repressive Syria; raised in Wisconsin. BS, University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee; MD, Medical College of Wisconsin, 1992. Served eleven years in the United States Navy as a medical officer, rising to lieutenant commander, including a posting as staff internist in the Office of the Attending Physician of the United States Congress; awarded the Meritorious Service Medal. Settled in Phoenix with his wife Gada in June 1999, joined his father’s medical practice and later founded the Jasser Center for Comprehensive Care, practicing internal medicine and nuclear cardiology for more than two decades. After the September 11 attacks he became a national voice for reform within Islam: he founded the American Islamic Forum for Democracy in 2003, which advocates the separation of mosque and state and opposes political Islam, co-founded the Center for Islamic Pluralism in 2004 and the Muslim Reform Movement, and organized in Phoenix what the Arizona Republic called the nation’s first Muslim rally against terrorism. He has testified before Congress, served as a commissioner on religious freedom, and is a frequent commentator. He and Gada have three children.

    Mark Lamb
    Arizona · 5th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Arizona’s 5th District and the likely next congressman: this is a safe Republican open seat that Rep. Andy Biggs gave up to run for governor. Lamb won the July 21, 2026 primary and had led polling by more than 35 points. The district covers much of the southeastern Valley including Gilbert, Queen Creek, Apache Junction, San Tan Valley and parts of Chandler and eastern Mesa. Previously served as the 24th Sheriff of Pinal County (January 2017–December 2024), succeeding Paul Babeu and running unopposed for re-election in 2020; he ran for the United States Senate in 2024 and lost the Republican primary to Kari Lake. Born July 14, 1972 in Hilo, Hawaii. Raised in a Latter-day Saint family in Hilo, Hawaii until age 11, then Manila, Panama and a two-year mission in Argentina; graduated high school in Chandler, Arizona and attended Dixie College, now Utah Tech University, where he played baseball. No military service. Ran a paintball business in Utah and worked in pest control after moving to Arizona in 2003, entering law enforcement in his thirties; he was valedictorian of the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office Deputy Academy. Spent six years with the Salt River Pima–Maricopa Indian Community police department, named Rookie of the Year, then Officer of the Year, then Detective of the Year in the Gang Enforcement Unit, and served on SWAT; he was a lead detective on a multi-agency federal RICO case that dismantled one of the East Valley’s most violent gangs, earning the Arizona Gang Investigators Association Award of Excellence, working gang enforcement and criminal investigations, before joining the Pinal County Sheriff’s Office in 2012; as sheriff he led an agency covering a county larger than Connecticut. Known nationally as “The American Sheriff,” he appeared on the television series Live PD and became prominent for refusing to enforce mask and vaccine mandates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Also a rancher. Endorsed by President Trump, Speaker Mike Johnson, former Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio, the National Association of Police Organizations and the Arizona Police Association. His campaign has been shadowed by allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies, and by earlier reported text messages; none has resulted in charges.

He has survived two of the closest races in the country: he beat Kirsten Engel 50.7-49.2 in 2022, then beat her again in 2024 by roughly 7,000 votes, 50.0% to 47.5%, in a race TOO CLOSE TO CALL FOR MORE THAN A WEEK — Engel led on election night before conceding. BORN AUGUST 31, 1982 IN HERMOSILLO, SONORA, MEXICO, and raised in Tucson; HE WAS THE FIRST IN HIS FAMILY TO GRADUATE FROM COLLEGE, attending PIMA COMMUNITY COLLEGE and earning his degree from the UNIVERSITY OF ARIZONA. No military service. Before Congress he was VICE PRESIDENT OF OUTREACH FOR THE TUCSON HISPANIC CHAMBER OF COMMERCE, then SENIOR ADVISER FOR REGIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS TO GOVERNOR DOUG DUCEY, and VICE CHAIR OF THE ARIZONA-MEXICO COMMISSION. HE DELIVERED THE REPUBLICAN RESPONSE TO THE 2023 STATE OF THE UNION IN SPANISH. He has signed the Americans for Tax Reform Taxpayer Protection Pledge and the U.S. Term Limits pledge, and TURNED DOWN both a 2024 Senate run and a 2026 governor run to stay in the House. He RAISED $1.14 MILLION IN THE FIRST QUARTER of 2026 and, like his opponent, was unopposed in the July 21 primary. HIS 2026 CHALLENGER IS DIFFERENT FROM THE LAST TWO: JoAnna Mendoza, a NAVY AND MARINE CORPS VETERAN who grew up in the district. The seat covers parts of Tucson and much of rural southeastern Arizona; note the internal split — he took 65.0% in Cochise County in 2024 while the district overall was a coin flip. He and his wife Laura have SIX CHILDREN.

    Daniel Butierez
    Arizona · 7th District
    Biography
    Painting contractor; the 2024 and 2025 Republican nominee in this district. Faces Democratic Rep. Adelita Grijalva. This is his THIRD consecutive contest for the seat. He was the Republican nominee against Rep. Raúl Grijalva in 2024, taking 36.6%; when Grijalva DIED OF LUNG CANCER COMPLICATIONS IN MARCH 2025, Butierez won the July 15 special primary with 60.8% over restaurant owner Jorge Rivas and off-road vehicle businessman Jimmy Rodriguez, then lost the SEPTEMBER 23, 2025 SPECIAL ELECTION to Grijalva’s daughter Adelita, 68.9% to 29.4% on 23.2% turnout. He now faces her again for the full term. A CONTRACTOR AND SMALL BUSINESS OWNER who owns a painting company and a second business. HIS BACKGROUND IS UNUSUAL AND HE CAMPAIGNS ON IT: he was WRONGFULLY CONVICTED AND SPENT TEN YEARS IN JAIL, and after clearing his name built a business giving second chances to people battling addiction or recently released from prison. His formal education and any military service are not published. Campaigns on border security — the district runs hundreds of miles along the Mexican border through Tucson, Yuma and Nogales into the Phoenix area — along with tax cuts, crime, drug abuse and homelessness. Democrats hold nearly a two-to-one registration advantage. Adelita Grijalva served on the Pima County Board of Supervisors and the Tucson Unified School District board, and won the 2025 Democratic primary with 61.4% over Deja Foxx and Daniel Hernández Jr.

Enlisted in the U.S. Army straight out of high school and served from 1985 to 1989 as an explosive ordnance disposal technician with the 56th Ordnance Detachment at Fort Indiantown Gap, reaching sergeant in under three years and earning the Army Achievement Medal, the Army Good Conduct Medal and the Explosive Ordnance Disposal Badge, with service in Southwest Asia. Competed in rodeos through college until a career-ending injury in 1993, then turned to announcing and producing them and performing as a country music singer. A news anchor and agricultural reporter at KAIT-TV in Jonesboro, he founded and ran the AgWatch Network, a farm news radio service carried on more than 50 affiliates across five states. Chairman of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence since January 2025, appointed by Speaker Mike Johnson; also Vice Chairman of Transportation and Infrastructure and a senior member of Agriculture. Born at Homestead Air Force Base to an Air Force family. Authored the Safe and Accurate Food Labeling Act.

    Incumbent representing Arkansas’s 2nd District since January 2015, succeeding Tim Griffin; the 22nd member of Congress to represent central Arkansas. No prior elected office. Bush administration as Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Treasury for Corporate Finance (1989–1991), where he was a U.S. negotiator in the bilateral Structural Impediments Initiative talks with Japan, and as executive secretary to the President’s Economic Policy Council (1991–1993). Past president of the Rotary Club of Little Rock and 2013 chairman of the Little Rock Regional Chamber of Commerce; served 15 years on the board of Arkansas Children’s Hospital and received the Distinguished Eagle Scout Award in 2019. A ninth-generation Arkansan and only child, born and living in Little Rock.     Biography
    Incumbent representing Arkansas’s 3rd District since January 2011, succeeding John Boozman. Decorated with the Legion of Merit, the Meritorious Service Medal with oak leaf cluster, the Army Commendation and Achievement Medals, the Global War on Terror Expeditionary and Service Medals and the Arkansas Distinguished Service Medal; inducted into the Arkansas Officer Candidate School Hall of Fame in 2011. Chairman of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Transportation, Housing and Urban Development; chaired the House Budget Committee in 2018 and was its ranking member from 2019 to 2021.     Ray Riehle
    California · 4th District
    Did not advance
    Biography
    Did NOT advance to the November ballot. Ray Riehle led early returns in the June 2, 2026 top-two primary for California’s 4th District with 23.9% to Democrat Eric Jones’s 21%, but Jones passed him as the count finished, so the two November places went to Democrats and there is no Republican on the ballot in this district. Rep. Mike Thompson, a 14-term incumbent first elected in 1998, led with 37.4% and faces Jones in a Democrat-versus-Democrat general. Riehle was the best-funded Republican in the field, reporting more than $108,000 by mid-April, and five other Republicans and one unaligned candidate each took under 6%. He originally launched in the 6th District and refiled for the 4th after Proposition 50 redrew the map and other candidates shuffled their plans; the new 4th stretches from Rohnert Park and Petaluma east across Napa, Yolo and Colusa counties through the northern Sacramento suburbs to Yuba City and the Sierra foothills, taking in all or parts of nine counties. Forecasters rate it Solid Democratic. No prior partisan elected office; he was appointed about ten years ago to the Citrus Heights Water District Board of Directors, where he says he learned about governance, and has served on the Citrus Heights Chamber of Commerce board and a bond oversight committee for the San Juan Unified School District. A Sacramento-area small business owner from Citrus Heights who says he is not a career politician. Campaigned on long-range infrastructure planning, arguing for a fifty- to hundred-year vision for roads, bridges, dams and energy, and on an America First agenda. Endorsed by a range of Republican groups and Sacramento city officials. In a notable turn, on August 17, 2026 he endorsed Eric Jones — the Democrat who edged him out — over Thompson, saying he had met Jones repeatedly and found alignment on water, PG&E issues and rebuilding trust in government; Thompson’s campaign responded that neither Jones nor Riehle is from the district.

    Republican nominee for California’s 13th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Adam Gray, who won the seat in 2024 by 187 votes out of more than 200,000 cast — the closest House result in California and an NRCC target. Previously served as the 80th Mayor of Stockton (2021–2025), winning in 2020 by unseating Democratic incumbent Michael Tubbs; he did not seek a second term, running instead for the 9th District against Rep. Josh Harder in 2024 and losing. AA in business, University of Phoenix; BS in business management, Grand Canyon University; MA in executive leadership, Liberty University. Joined the United States Marine Corps in 2001, months before the September 11 attacks, and was later recruited by the White House Military Office and assigned to Marine One during the George W. Bush administration. After leaving the service he spent eight years with one of the country’s largest private security firms in Silicon Valley, rising to district manager with a $55 million annual budget and more than 1,300 employees; in 2013 he resigned to become full-time executive administrative pastor at a Stockton church, running its finances and daily operations, and served as director of operations for a local antipoverty nonprofit. As mayor he oversaw Stockton’s post-bankruptcy recovery and its pandemic response, saw violent crime and homicides fall, expanded homelessness services, and invested more than $6 million in youth programming and workforce development with fourteen community organizations, employing over 600 young people. Endorsed as mayor by the Stockton Police Officers’ Association and the professional firefighters’ local. A third-generation Stocktonian and the grandson of a Mexican immigrant; he and his wife Bonnie have been married more than twenty years and have two children. The new district covers all of Merced County, most of Madera, and parts of Stanislaus, Fresno and San Joaquin.     Biography
    Republican incumbent for California’s 22nd District since 2023; he previously held the 21st District 2013-2019 and 2021-2023. HE IS THE MOST EXPOSED REPUBLICAN IN THE HOUSE AND THE ONE MEMBER WHO HAS ALREADY LOST A SEAT IN AN ANTI-TRUMP WAVE: TJ Cox beat him in 2018 and he won it back in 2020. He has won FIVE OF HIS SIX CONGRESSIONAL RACES SINCE 2012 in a San Joaquin Valley district where REGISTERED DEMOCRATS SIGNIFICANTLY OUTNUMBER REPUBLICANS. Born David Goncalves Valadao on April 14, 1977 in HANFORD. HIS FAMILY ARE PORTUGUESE IMMIGRANTS FROM THE AZORES: his father Eduardo, the youngest of eight, grew up helping run the family dairy there, came to California in 1969 and started a Central Valley dairy in 1973; as a teenager David bucked hay and fed the cows every morning before school. Hanford High School, 1995; COLLEGE OF THE SEQUOIAS, Visalia, 1996-1998. No military service. A DAIRY FARMER — the family business now runs two dairies and more than 1,000 acres in Kings County — and he knows the risk first-hand, HAVING ONCE DECLARED BANKRUPTCY to absolve the farm’s delinquent loans. He held leadership roles on the CALIFORNIA MILK ADVISORY BOARD and the Western States Dairy Trade Association and chaired Land O’Lakes’ Regional Leadership Council. He served in the CALIFORNIA STATE ASSEMBLY 2010-2012 as vice chair of its Agriculture Committee. In the House he is CHAIRMAN OF THE APPROPRIATIONS SUBCOMMITTEE ON THE LEGISLATIVE BRANCH and sits on its Agriculture and Defense subcommittees, and HE CHAIRS THE REPUBLICAN GOVERNANCE GROUP, the House’s centrist Republican bloc, succeeding David Joyce in 2025 — the single most important fact about how he operates. To Central Valley farmers he is simply “David,” and that local identity is his entire pitch: his first 2026 television advertisement declares “David Valadao is on our side.” THE 2026 RISK IS REAL AND HIS OWN SIDE SEES IT: a longtime Fresno County farmer and registered Democrat who has voted Republican before told CalMatters, “unfortunately, David Valadao’s vote could be the one that gives Trump the power.” He has consistently DECLINED CalMatters’ interview requests.     Biography
    Republican nominee for California’s 24th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Salud Carbajal, who has held the seat since 2017; Smith took 39.5% to Carbajal’s 52.5% in the four-candidate June 2, 2026 top-two primary. Campaigns on housing costs and the district’s cost of living, government waste, and the argument that long-tenured officeholders across the Central Coast have delivered little; he has said Carbajal is a decent man and that the race is not about his character.     Biography
    Republican nominee for California’s 26th District, advancing from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary out of a nine-candidate field; the Ventura County district takes in Oxnard, Thousand Oaks, Simi Valley, Camarillo and Calabasas. A lifelong Californian who raised his family in Thousand Oaks over twenty years before moving to Oxnard, where he has lived for seventeen; he and his wife Toni have three children and nine grandchildren.

    California · 32nd District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for California’s 32nd District, challenging Democratic Rep. Brad Sherman, who has served in Congress since 1997. In an unexpected result, Thompson finished FIRST in the nine-candidate June 2, 2026 top-two primary, taking 48,317 votes to Sherman’s 47,037 — 37% to 36% — as the only Republican in a field with seven other Democrats; he led decisively in the Ventura County portion while Sherman led in Los Angeles County. Under the new maps Simi Valley was moved into the district, joining Malibu and much of the San Fernando Valley across parts of Ventura and Los Angeles counties. The seat is nonetheless rated D+17. This is his second run here: he was the 2024 nominee and lost to Sherman 66.2% to 33.8%, though he took 47.4% in Ventura County. He also ran in the 37th District in 2020. Born in Clarksdale, Mississippi, in about 1945. BBA, University of Mississippi, 1966; JD, University of Mississippi School of Law, 1968. Served in the United States Army Reserve, Adjutant General’s Corps, from 1968 to 1974. A Malibu attorney, talent manager and film producer, and a member of the California Bar. Unanimously endorsed by the California Republican Party and the Los Angeles County Republican Party, and also by the Ventura County Republican Party, the American Independent Party, California College Republicans, and by Brock Pierce of the Bitcoin Foundation and Perianne Boring of the Chamber of Digital Commerce. Campaigns on lowering taxes, including a challenge to the Los Angeles Measure ULA transfer tax, border security and comprehensive immigration reform, affordability, homelessness, and what he calls a new civil conversation that stops identifying people solely by political affiliation. At 81 he is among the oldest nominees in the country. His certified ballot designation on the California Secretary of State’s November 3, 2026 general election list is “Attorney/Film Producer”.

    Biography
    Republican nominee for California’s 37th District, having advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary in second place behind Democratic Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove. Nine candidates ran, tying this district with two others for the largest House field in Los Angeles County this cycle; Kamlager-Dove took roughly 54% and Fedalizo about 14%, ahead of Democrat Samantha Mota on 10%. The district covers south and southwest Los Angeles, South Vermont and Culver City, and its shape changed little under Proposition 50. Kamlager-Dove has held the seat since 2023, succeeding Karen Bass, after serving in the California Assembly and State Senate. He goes by Bong. No elected office held; he ran for this same seat in 2024, losing as a write-in in the March primary, and ran for the Los Angeles Community College Board of Trustees later that year, losing the general election for Seat No. 1. Of Native American and Filipino heritage. Holds an MBA. Served in the United States Navy. An entrepreneur: a Subway franchise owner named Franchisee of the Year in 2005, founder of Pow Wow on Parade, and senior vice president and now executive director of Nature’s Hotline Food Bank; he has also received awards for entrepreneurial work in the biofuel industry. In 2017 he was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize for his work helping formerly incarcerated people find employment. Lives in Los Angeles.

    Biography
    Incumbent in the House since January 1993, now serving his seventeenth term; California redistricting has changed his district number several times; elected most recently in the 41st, he appears in the 40th on the 2026 ballot under the Proposition 50 map. Trump carried the district by under two points in 2024. Democrats’ top House super PAC has already reserved millions in advertising. Born Timothy Gabriel Joseph Evans on July 28, 1986 in Aurora, Colorado; he lives on a FAMILY FARM IN FORT LUPTON, which he owns and operates. BA, PATRICK HENRY COLLEGE, 2009. UNITED STATES ARMY 2007-2019, RETIRING AS A CAPTAIN, serving in the Virginia and COLORADO ARMY NATIONAL GUARD and deploying in the WAR IN AFGHANISTAN under Operation Enduring Freedom. He then spent A DECADE AS A POLICE OFFICER WITH THE ARVADA POLICE DEPARTMENT, 2011-2022, RISING TO LIEUTENANT, and is a concealed carry firearms instructor. HE IS HISPANIC. Served one term in the COLORADO HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES for the 48th district, 2023-2025, on the Judiciary and Energy and Environment committees, and was ENDORSED BY PRESIDENT TRUMP in 2024, beating former state Rep. Janak Joshi in that primary. In this Congress he sponsored the RATEPAYER PROTECTION ACT, which was ORDERED REPORTED OUT OF ENERGY AND COMMERCE 52-0 in July 2026 with 35 cosponsors. He faces Democrat MANNY RUTINEL in November. NOTE FOR CONTEXT: Caraveo announced a comeback bid in April 2025 but WITHDREW IN SEPTEMBER 2025, citing her struggle with mental health and the stigmatization of mental health issues. Also on the record: Evans FIRED HIS 2024 CAMPAIGN POLITICAL DIRECTOR in September 2024 after reporting on her history of promoting political violence. Married to Anne since 2010, with two children.

    Uncontested for the Republican nomination in the August 11, 2026 primary. She faces former Hartford mayor Luke Bronin, who unseated 28-year Democratic incumbent John Larson in the primary with 54% of a four-way race — so this is an open-seat contest against a new Democratic nominee, not a run at a long-serving incumbent. She completed Ballotpedia’s Candidate Connection survey in 2025.

    Republican nominee in Connecticut’s 4th District and the party’s 2024 nominee for the same seat. No prior elected office. A Greenwich ophthalmic surgeon and attorney.     Dan Green
    Florida · 9th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Florida’s 9th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Darren Soto, who has held the central Florida seat since 2017. The Almanac of American Politics lists Green among expected members of the next Congress. He won a seven-candidate August 18, 2026 primary with about 25.4%, narrowly edging rancher Ben Butler on 24.4%; the Associated Press did not call it until two days after the election. Former Osceola School Board member and retired colonel Thomas Chalifoux, who was the 2024 nominee and entered with a $3 million war chest, took about 20%, and Orlando businessman Jorge Martinez about 19%. The race exists because Florida’s mid-decade redistricting dismantled Soto’s Hispanic-majority seat, which had been protected under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and was one of four in the state redrawn to favor Republicans. The district shifted from a 51–48 Kamala Harris win in 2024 to one President Trump would have carried 58–41, and from a four-point Democratic voter-registration advantage to a six-point Republican one. It now covers Osceola, Highlands, Indian River, Okeechobee and Glades counties plus parts of Orange and Polk, with much of the Democratic-leaning Orlando core moved into a neighboring district. Soto has accused Governor DeSantis and Republican legislators of violating Florida’s Fair Districts Amendments, the constitutional provisions voters approved in 2010 barring maps drawn to favor a party or incumbent; Republicans defend the map, which remains in place. The University of Virginia’s Center for Politics rates the race Likely Republican. An Indian River County resident. No prior elected office. A military veteran and former Defense Department official who has stressed a past appointment by President Trump.

    Mike Beltran
    Florida · 14th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Florida’s 14th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor, who is seeking an eleventh term and is facing her first credible challenge since she was first elected in 2006. He won the August 18, 2026 primary with 45.6% over former state Rep. Kevin Steele on 30.2%, in a field of eight; the other six candidates each took under 10%. The race exists because of Florida’s mid-decade redistricting, pushed by Governor Ron DeSantis and passed by the Legislature, which shifted the district eastward: under the old lines Kamala Harris carried it 53.3–45.6, but under the new boundaries President Trump would have won it 54.7–44.2. It is one of 23 Democratic-held districts Trump carried in 2024. The NRCC has named it a target and the DCCC placed Castor in its Frontline program; Cook and Inside Elections both rate the general Toss-up, and Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved it from Safe Democratic to Leans Republican. The redrawn seat removes all of Pinellas County and much of Tampa, running from South Tampa east to the Polk County line and south to Manatee. Born June 26, 1984 in New York City and raised in Brooklyn; graduated Stuyvesant High School in 2002, earned a BA in international relations magna cum laude from the University of Pennsylvania in 2005, and a JD from Harvard Law School in 2008. No military service. Moved to Florida in 2010 and clerked for United States District Judge Steven D. Merryday, then practiced as an associate at Boies, Schiller and Flexner before founding his own firm, Beltran Litigation; he is licensed in Florida and New York, handles high-stakes civil and criminal litigation for individuals and small businesses, and has been recognized as an Outstanding Young Florida Lawyer. Appointed by Governors Rick Scott and Ron DeSantis to the Judicial Nominating Commission for Florida’s Thirteenth Circuit in Hillsborough County, and later to the commission for the Fifth District Court of Appeal; he secured authorization for four new county court judges in Hillsborough. Served in the Florida House of Representatives from 2018 to 2024, representing parts of this district; his legislation included restrictions on minors vaping near schools and a safe-haven law allowing parents to surrender infants anonymously to hospital staff, and in 2023 he filed an amendment to permit open carry of firearms before withdrawing it under pressure from legislative leaders. Calls himself “MAGA Mike” and campaigns against federal overspending, while also saying he crossed party lines more than any other member of the Florida House and that bipartisan cooperation will matter in a closely divided Congress. He has emphasized being from East Hillsborough and having won elections there. The primary drew complaints when the Hillsborough County Republican Executive Committee distributed voter guides with his name underlined.     Sydney Gruters
    Florida · 16th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Florida’s newly redrawn 16th District and the likely next member: the Almanac of American Politics lists her among expected members of the next Congress. The seat is open because Rep. Vern Buchanan announced on January 27, 2026 that he would retire after ten terms and nearly two decades; he was a senior Republican on Ways and Means, though he lost a bid for its chairmanship. Gruters won the August 18, 2026 primary with more than 63% over Navy veteran and educator Ed Pope and Eddie Speir, founder of Inspiration Academy and a former New College trustee who had taken just under 40% against Buchanan in the 2024 primary. She faces Democrat Kelly Kirschner, a former Sarasota mayor, in November. Trump urged her to run on Truth Social in March and gave a “complete and total endorsement” before she had even filed; she also drew backing from Speaker Mike Johnson, Senate leadership, local sheriffs, Buchanan himself and Maggie’s List, and raised more than $1 million. No elected office held. No military service. A career congressional and government staffer: she began as a congressional aide in 2004 and spent more than a decade in Buchanan’s offices, later serving as district director for Rep. Greg Steube and, during President Trump’s first administration, as State Director for USDA Rural Development in Florida and the U.S. Virgin Islands; she is now vice president of advancement and executive director of the New College Foundation in Sarasota. Her husband, Joe Gruters, is a Florida state senator and CHAIR OF THE REPUBLICAN NATIONAL COMMITTEE. Campaigns on the cost of living — groceries, gas, housing and insurance — and on constituent service, arguing her staff experience lets her help residents with Social Security, veterans’ benefits and disaster assistance from day one. She has acknowledged starting the race without deep ties in parts of the district and spent the campaign building them, while her USDA work gave her connections among farmers in Hardee and DeSoto counties. A working mother of three.     Jim Schwartzel
    Florida · 19th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Florida’s 19th District and the likely next congressman: the Almanac of American Politics lists him among expected members of the next Congress. He won the August 18, 2026 primary over nine other Republicans for this Southwest Florida seat, open because Rep. Byron Donalds gave it up to run for governor. President Trump carried the district decisively in 2024 under the map enacted by Governor Ron DeSantis. The field drew national attention: CNN previewed it as “a ’clown show’ of carpetbaggers and characters,” and Schwartzel defeated two men who had previously served in the House from other states — former Rep. Chris Collins of New York — along with former Illinois state senator Jim Oberweis, Catalina Lauf, Ola Hawatmeh, John Strand, Greg Bukowski, Mike Pedersen and Linda Sawyer. No prior elected office. Born in Naples; graduated Bishop Verot High School and earned a bachelor’s degree from Stetson University in 1998. No military service. A Southwest Florida media executive: president of Fort Myers-based Sun Broadcasting, owner and operator of the conservative talk station 92.5 FOX News, and owner of Gulfshore Life Media. Campaigns on low taxes, cutting regulation, small business, border security and federal spending, and on water quality — an avid boater, he has made protecting the Caloosahatchee River and the region’s beaches a priority. His campaign describes him as “not a career politician with ambitions for higher office.” A lifelong Southwest Floridian; he and his wife Carly, his high school sweetheart, have two children.

    Biography
    Republican nominee for Florida’s newly drawn 22nd District, an open seat after six-term Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel chose to seek re-election in the neighboring 23rd once the new map took effect. He won the August 18, 2026 primary over a crowded and well-funded field that included Keiser University Vice Chancellor Belinda Keiser, fintech entrepreneur Michael Carbonara and Marine veteran David Burck; seven Republicans and two Democrats qualified. The district was substantially redrawn under the mid-decade map Governor Ron DeSantis signed in May 2026, now stretching from inland Palm Beach County through Wellington and the Glades, across western Broward including Parkland and Weston, through Hendry County and west to Collier County and Marco Island. Coral Springs was split in half, packing Democratic voters into the 20th and draining them from the 22nd. The seat moved from safely Democratic to R+4 on Cook’s index; Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted it from Safe Democratic to Leans Republican. Frankel won it 55–45 in 2024 under the old lines. No prior elected office; he sought the Republican nomination in the 19th District in 2022, losing to Byron Donalds and afterward suing him. Served in the United States Marine Corps. A Naples businessman and food industry entrepreneur who came to the United States as a child refugee from Iraq. Endorsed by Rep. Gus Bilirakis, Collier County Sheriff Kevin Rambosk, former Florida Senate President Kathleen Passidomo and the Marco Island Council chair. He has proposed renaming a stretch of Interstate 75 the “President Donald J. Trump Interstate.” During the primary an anonymous website backing a rival attacked his postgraduate education, military service and the fact that he lives at the opposite end of the district. He faces Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal and White House Fellow endorsed by Frankel and EMILY’s List, in a race expected to draw national attention.

    Republican nominee for Florida’s 24th District, an open South Florida seat after Rep. Frederica Wilson announced her retirement in May 2026; Wilson had held it since 2011 and won 2024 comfortably.     Biography
    Republican nominee for Florida’s newly drawn 25th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz; he won the August 18, 2026 primary over four other Republicans — Dan Franzese, Joe Kaufman, George Moraitis and Raven Harrison. The district was created when the Florida Legislature approved a new map in April 2026 and runs along the southeast coast from Delray Beach through Boca Raton and Deerfield Beach into parts of Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood and Miami Beach, taking in Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties; handicappers have described it as lean Republican to toss-up. His campaign reported raising a record $1.3 million in the first quarter. Served on the Boca Raton City Council from 2014, was re-elected in 2017 and appointed deputy mayor, and became Mayor of Boca Raton on April 27, 2018 after Governor Rick Scott suspended his predecessor; he was elected in his own right and served three terms until term limits ended his tenure in 2026, winning re-election with 89% of the vote. Chairs the America First Policy Institute’s Mayors’ Council, a national group of mayors. Born in Miami Beach and raised in Fort Lauderdale; attended Pine Crest School, graduated cum laude from Harvard with a bachelor’s degree in government, and earned his JD at Georgetown University Law Center. No military service. Began as a commercial litigator, then opened his own law practice and two other small businesses serving entrepreneurs; holds Martindale-Hubbell’s AV Preeminent rating. As mayor he voted seven consecutive times to lower the property tax rate, kept police starting salaries among the highest in the country, and secured Boca Raton’s first new public school in decades. Campaigns on affordability, insurance and tax reform, deregulation, border security and opposition to antisemitism. He and his wife Bella have two children.

    Jim Kingston
    Georgia · 1st District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Georgia’s 1st District and the likely next congressman: the Almanac of American Politics lists him among expected members of the next Congress. The Savannah-area seat is open because six-term Rep. Buddy Carter ran for the Senate instead, losing that primary in a landslide to Mike Collins and Derek Dooley. Fourteen candidates entered — six Republicans and eight Democrats — and Kingston won the nomination outright on May 19, 2026 with 52%, avoiding a runoff; former Chatham County Commissioner Pat Farrell was second with 17%, Kandiss Taylor third with 13%. President Trump carried the district 58–42 in 2024 and its Cook rating is R+8; Republicans have held it since 1993. No prior elected office — he has never run for or held one. Born James Morris Kingston about 1991, the youngest of four children, and raised in Savannah. Attended St. Andrew’s School, where he was class president and a team captain in football and baseball, then the University of Georgia, enrolled from 2009 to 2015; reporting by The Current states he did not graduate. No military service. A commercial insurance executive, senior vice president at Marsh McLennan, with successive insurance industry jobs since 2015; he has also spent a decade working behind the scenes for Georgia Republican campaigns, organizing meet-and-greets and driving candidates between events. Trump’s endorsement described him as a “MAGA warrior” and “a very successful Businessman, Civic Leader, and Conservative Activist.” He is the son of Jack Kingston, who held this same seat for 22 years from 1993 to 2015, rose to a senior position on the Appropriations Committee and served as Vice Chair of the House Republican Conference before running unsuccessfully for the Senate in 2014; the Almanac notes the younger Kingston began the race relatively unknown but benefited from residual goodwill toward his father. Building on that name and his father’s network he assembled a formidable war chest, reporting $1.38 million on hand at the end of 2025, more than double the rest of the field combined, and drew backing from Club for Growth and from Rep. Jim Jordan, who campaigned for him in Savannah. He has said rising costs were the biggest issue facing the district. His primary opponents criticized him as having a thin résumé and trading on his father’s name; The Current also reported that his voter registration lists a Chatham County home owned by his mother with a mailing address in Atlanta. He is endorsed by state Senator Ben Watson, his uncle by marriage. He married Meredith Lee of Savannah in February 2026.

    Biography
    Republican nominee for Georgia’s 2nd District, challenging Democratic Rep. Sanford Bishop, who has held the southwest Georgia seat since 1993 and is serving his seventeenth term; Bishop is the dean of Georgia’s congressional delegation, a member of the Blue Dog Coalition, and ran unopposed in his own primary. He won the four-way March 17, 2026 primary with about 48.5% over Rocio Cleveland, Paul Friedman and Mark Su, running a grassroots door-to-door campaign, and acknowledged afterwards that he had NOT YET FILED A STATEMENT OF CANDIDACY WITH THE FEC. He was also the 2018 nominee here, losing to Jan Schakowsky 73.5% to 26.5%. No elected office held, and he says so himself: “I’ve been in Chicagoland public service for 40 years as a pastor. I have never held a government office.” He is PASTOR OF LAKEWOOD CHAPEL IN ARLINGTON HEIGHTS. HIS POSITIONING IS THE MOST STRIKING THING ON THIS CARD AND A MEMBER SHOULD KNOW IT BEFORE MEETING HIM. He calls immigration his top issue and wants BIPARTISAN COMPREHENSIVE LEGISLATION — “it’s going to take both parties coming up with something fair… I’m the kind of guy that gets along with both sides” — and promises to “make it a hallmark to cross the aisle.” AND HE HAS PUBLICLY QUESTIONED PRESIDENT TRUMP: “maybe Trump’s not even a conservative… now I’m starting to have a hard time with Trump, because if he loses people like me… he has to be careful.” He argues his party is not tolerant enough to grow its base in places like Chicago, and raises mental health and addiction as priorities. THE SEAT IS OPEN: Schakowsky, 81, retires in January after 28 years. DANIEL BISS, MAYOR OF EVANSTON, won a FOURTEEN-WAY Democratic primary with about 29%, ahead of Kat Abughazaleh on 26% and state Senator Laura Fine on 20%, endorsed by Schakowsky and Senator Elizabeth Warren. NO REPUBLICAN HAS REPRESENTED THIS DISTRICT SINCE 1947. Elleson on his own odds: “competition is good… even if the Democrats end up winning, it’s just good to be challenged.”

    Biography
    Projected winner of the Republican primary; faces Democratic Rep. Bill Foster, who was unopposed. He won a FOUR-WAY Republican primary on March 17, 2026, with NBC News projecting the result; Bill Foster ran unopposed for the Democrats. Currently ELBURN VILLAGE PRESIDENT — elected municipal office — and a business manager. A RETIRED UNITED STATES NAVY NON-COMMISSIONED OFFICER. Foster, for context, is a PARTICLE PHYSICIST who spent his career at Fermilab, holds a PhD from Harvard, and first entered the House in a March 2008 special election to replace former Speaker Dennis Hastert; he has represented the 11th since 2013. CORRECTION AND EXPANSION. He is not simply a “retired Navy NCO” and “village president”: HE IS A RETIRED UNITED STATES NAVY MASTER CHIEF PETTY OFFICER (E-9), the senior enlisted rank, having SERVED FROM 1978 TO 2000. The son of GERMAN IMMIGRANTS who came to America after the Second World War, he joined the Navy straight out of high school, earned a CRYPTOLOGY/LINGUIST RATING and spent NINE YEARS IN INTELLIGENCE as a radio-telephone intercept operator. Aged 65, born in TOLEDO, OHIO. EDUCATION: BACHELOR’S DEGREE, UNIVERSITY OF SOUTH FLORIDA, 1991; graduate degree, UNIVERSITY OF TOLEDO, 1997; graduate degree, NEW YORK INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, 2004 — a finance degree and an MBA. HIS ELECTED RECORD IS LONGER THAN THE CARD HAD IT: he joined the Elburn Village Board within three years of moving there in 2006, served as a VILLAGE TRUSTEE FROM 2009 TO 2017, and has been VILLAGE PRESIDENT SINCE 2017, RE-ELECTED TWICE. Career: a consultant, plant manager and general manager — at ACCENTURE he led multi-million-dollar IT and AI modernization programs across healthcare and telecom. He won the four-way March 17, 2026 primary with about 43%, 13,286 votes, over Naperville’s Mike Pierce, a retired Army lieutenant colonel, on 39%, plus Charlie Kim and Tedora Brown. He describes himself as CENTRIST and “practical,” campaigning on affordability, tax relief for the middle class, and lower energy and healthcare costs, and argues his mayoral experience shapes his focus: “as a mayor, I see firsthand how Washington policies affect water systems, roads, public safety, and budgets.” He supports President Trump’s economic plan including tariffs. He and his wife Carrie are Elburn Lions Club members and their family FOSTERS DOGS for Safe Haven Rescue.

He won the March 17, 2026 Republican primary over Joshua Loyd, a West Point graduate and Army veteran who was the party’s 2024 nominee and lost to Budzinski by 16 points; Wilson held a considerable fundraising lead.     Indiana · 1st District
    Biography
    Porter County Commissioner, in her third year representing the Center District; won the May 2026 Republican primary over small business owner David Ben Ruiz and former communications manager Jim Schenke. This is one of the few genuinely competitive House races in Indiana. Faces Rep. Frank Mrvan, first elected in 2020, who has survived close fights in the last two cycles. The district is trending Republican fast — Trump lost it by about 8 points in 2020 but narrowed that to under 1 point in 2024, and it now sits at Cook PVI D+1. Democrats have held the seat for roughly a century. THIS IS INDIANA’S ONLY GENUINELY COMPETITIVE HOUSE SEAT and national handicappers treat it as the state’s principal opportunity. She won the May 5, 2026 Republican primary with 45.8% over James “Jim” Schenke on 30.1% and David Ben Ruiz on 24.1%. A Valparaiso resident and the first Porter County resident nominated here in this century apart from one earlier case. PRIOR ELECTED OFFICE: SHE SERVED ON THE PORTER COUNTY BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. She built careers in TECHNOLOGY AND FINANCE, which she says taught her “the value of fiscal responsibility, transparency and careful decision-making.” Her formal education and any military service are not published. Campaigns on “safe cities, secure borders and smarter spending,” prioritizing American families and businesses over foreign interests, and reducing the national debt, arguing “for too long, Northwest Indiana has been represented by the same old political establishment.” THE NRCC IS BEHIND HER, calling her “a trusted local leader” poised to flip the seat and noting that IN-01 HAS SHIFTED RIGHT ROUGHLY 12% SINCE 2016: Trump improved his Lake County margin by nearly 15% over that period, and won Porter County by 7% in 2020 and by over 10% in 2024. The district is now D+1 — down from D+3 — and in 2024 it was INDIANA’S ONLY CONGRESSIONAL DISTRICT DECIDED BY UNDER TEN POINTS. It covers Lake and Porter counties and northwest LaPorte, the Indiana portion of the Chicago metro, with an industrial history and strong organized labor presence. Mrvan, seeking a fourth term, succeeded the long-serving Pete Visclosky in 2021 and sits on Appropriations subcommittees; his father Frank Mrvan Jr. served in the Indiana Senate for decades. Write-in independents Alexander Degman and James Johnson are also on the ballot. RACE STATUS, ONE SOURCE, ONE DATE: 270toWin’s mirror of the COOK POLITICAL REPORT ratings, current as of AUGUST 25, 2026, lists this district among the MOST COMPETITIVE 2026 RACES (a category that includes seats favored to flip). Cards in this file that carry no rating are NOT thereby safe — see the ledger note on the ratings pass.

DIRECTOR OF THE IOWA DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC HEALTH 2010-2013 and a state senator 2019-2020.     Biography
    Republican nominee for Iowa’s 4th District and the likely next congressman: forecasters rate this northwest Iowa seat Solid Republican, and he ran unopposed for the nomination in the June 2, 2026 primary. The seat is open because Rep. Randy Feenstra gave it up to run for governor, losing that primary to Zach Lahn in June. President Trump carried Iowa by more than 13 points in 2024 and won 35 of the district’s 36 counties. He faces Democrat Dave Dawson, a former state lawmaker. No prior elected office; he announced on June 25, 2025, the first candidate of either party in the race, under the banner “America First, Iowa Always.” Born about 1967, one of five children in an Irish Catholic family in Sioux City; his father was a longtime family physician and a founding director of the Siouxland Medical Education Foundation’s family practice residency program, and his mother a teacher and 4-H leader. Elected student body president at Bishop Heelan High School, and as a junior in 1984 was chosen for the American Legion’s Boys Nation program, where he met President Ronald Reagan at a White House Rose Garden ceremony and was called on to ask a question. Bachelor’s degree from St. John’s University in Collegeville, Minnesota, with a double major in government and management; Juris Doctor from the Ave Maria School of Law in Ann Arbor, Michigan, during which he worked in both the civil and criminal divisions of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Michigan. He passed the Iowa bar and is a licensed attorney, though he has never practiced law. Served in the Iowa Air National Guard. Worked as a Fortune 500 account executive in sales for Honeywell before law school. Spent more than twenty years promoting northwest Iowa: president of the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce and of The Siouxland Initiative since 2011, covering a tri-state region around Sioux City, and chair of the statewide Iowa Chamber Alliance; his organizations say they helped bring in billions in capital investment and create thousands of jobs. Earlier a longtime political consultant for Republican candidates and worked part-time for the United States Department of Justice. On the use of military force he says the federal government must be “extremely prudent” about entering wars, citing his own Air National Guard service and the fact that five of his six children currently serve in the United States military.

    Ed Gallrein
    Kentucky · 4th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Kentucky’s 4th District and the likely next congressman: Cook and Inside Elections both rate the general Solid Republican, and he faces Democrat Melissa Strange. He got there by defeating seven-term incumbent Rep. Thomas Massie in the May 19, 2026 primary — described as the most expensive primary in U.S. congressional history, and the only House primary of the cycle in which President Trump endorsed a challenger to a sitting Republican. Massie was the second House member to lose a primary in 2026. Trump asked Gallrein to run and endorsed him on October 17, 2025, days before he announced on October 21; the President traveled to northern Kentucky in March to campaign for him, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appeared with him the day before the vote in what the Pentagon said was a personal capacity. An advertising blitz funded largely by pro-Trump and pro-Israel groups backed the effort. Gallrein carried Boone, Kenton and Campbell counties across the river from Cincinnati and Oldham County in the Louisville suburbs, which together make up most of the district vote; Massie led only in his home county of Lewis, and by a smaller margin than in his last contested primary. The Associated Press called it at 7:54 p.m. Born Edward Gibson Gallrein III on April 20, 1958 in Shelbyville, Kentucky, and originally from Simpson County. Graduated Franklin-Simpson High School in 1975 and was inducted into its Athletic Hall of Fame; attended Centre College, playing varsity football, then Murray State University for a BS in agriculture in 1981 and an MS in agriculture and agribusiness economics in 1984, playing football there too. Later earned an MS in financial management with honors from the Naval Postgraduate School and an MS in strategic studies with distinction from the Air War College, and graduated the Air Command and Staff College and the Armed Forces Staff College. No prior elected office; he ran for the Kentucky Senate in 2024 and narrowly lost the primary to Aaron Reed. Served thirty years in the United States Navy, from 1984 to 2014, retiring as a captain; a SEAL officer who was also Army Ranger qualified, he led seven SEAL teams and units including multiple tours with SEAL Team Six, deploying from Panama to the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan and Iraq. His decorations include three Bronze Star Medals, two Presidential Unit Citations, multiple Combat Action awards, and the Army Combat Parachutist Badge with Bronze Star and Bronze Arrowhead for a combat parachute assault — his campaign says he is the only Navy SEAL ever to earn that device. A fifth-generation Kentucky farmer whose family has worked the land for over a century, now running The Circle G Farm and Stables near Shelbyville. Endorsed by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Registered as an independent from 2016 to 2021. A father of four and grandfather of four. Campaigned on unequivocal support for the President’s agenda, saying “this district is Trump Country” and that the President needs backup rather than obstacles in Congress. Massie’s defeat came six months after the Epstein Files Transparency Act became law, an issue that had defined much of his final term.

    Biography
    House Majority Leader and incumbent representing Louisiana’s 1st District since May 2008, when he won the special election to succeed Bobby Jindal. Previously served in the Louisiana House of Representatives (1996–2007) and the Louisiana Senate (2008). Graduated Archbishop Rummel High School, 1983; BS in computer science with a political science minor, Louisiana State University, 1989, where he was twice elected speaker of the Student Assembly. No military service. Worked as a software engineer and later as a marketing executive for a technology company before entering politics. Led House passage of the 2012 RESTORE Act, directing Deepwater Horizon Clean Water Act fines to coastal restoration. Critically wounded in the June 14, 2017 congressional baseball practice shooting and returned to Congress after a long recovery; he wrote a book about it, Back in the Game (2018). As Majority Leader he holds no standing committee assignments. Louisiana canceled its May 2026 congressional primaries after the Supreme Court’s Callais ruling; all candidates now appear on a single November 3 all-candidate ballot, with a December 12 runoff if nobody clears 50%. He won outright on the 2024 November ballot against Mel Manuel, Randall Arrington, Ross Shales and Frankie Hyers.
    2026 redistricting & election structure
    Louisiana has no U.S. House nominees, and will not have any before Election Day. The Supreme Court ruled in Louisiana v. Callais on April 29, 2026 that the state’s map was an unconstitutional gerrymander. On April 30 Gov. Jeff Landry signed Executive Order 26-038 suspending the U.S. House closed party primaries set for May 16 and the June 27 runoff; the Senate primary proceeded. House races stayed on the ballot during early voting but those votes were voided and are not counted. The Legislature then passed a new map dismantling one of the state’s two majority-Black districts, likely flipping a Democratic-held seat. Under the replacement schedule the U.S. House primary is a jungle primary held Nov. 3, 2026 — the same day as the general election elsewhere — with runoffs Dec. 12, 2026. So Louisiana seats will not be decided on election night, and any candidate here is a primary entrant, not a party nominee. Several lawsuits contest the suspension. Sources: Office of the Governor of Louisiana, FEC, NBC News, Axios New Orleans.

Became widely known for the sheriff’s office Crime Stoppers videos, in which he addressed suspects directly; the series drew millions of views, earned him the nickname the Cajun John Wayne, and led many suspects to turn themselves in. Chairman of the Oversight and Government Reform Subcommittee on Federal Law Enforcement and a senior member of that committee; also serves on Armed Services, on its Seapower and Projection Forces and Readiness subcommittees. A core member of the House Freedom Caucus. Born in New Orleans, the seventh of eight children, and raised in Covington on a family farm that raised and trained horses; his district takes in Lafayette, Lake Charles and New Iberia.

    Speaker of the House and incumbent representing Louisiana’s 4th District since December 2016, when he won by the largest margin in his region in more than 50 years; now in his fifth term, representing about 760,000 residents across 20 parishes. Previously served in the Louisiana House of Representatives (2015–2017). Graduated Captain Shreve High School, Shreveport; BS in business administration, Louisiana State University, 1995, where he was president of the LSU Interfraternity Council and vice president of Kappa Sigma; JD, LSU’s Paul M. Hebert Law Center, 1998, where he was class president, founder and president of the Christian Legal Society, and a member of the National Moot Court team. No military service; the eldest son of a Shreveport firefighter who was critically burned and permanently disabled in the line of duty, and the first person in his family to attend college. Practiced constitutional law for nearly 20 years, litigating high-profile cases in district and appellate courts nationwide; an attorney and spokesman for the Alliance Defense Fund, later Alliance Defending Freedom (2002–2010), a senior attorney and partner at Kitchens Law Firm in Minden, and founding dean of the Pressler School of Law at Louisiana College in 2010. The 56th Speaker, elected in October 2023 — the first Louisianan ever to hold the office, the highest-ranked official in the state’s history, the second fastest member ever elevated to the post at under 6.8 years’ service, and the first person unanimously elected to it by his party in more than two decades. Previously Vice Chairman of the House Republican Conference and Chairman of the Republican Study Committee, and chairman of the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Limited Government. As Speaker he holds no standing committee assignments. Louisiana suspended its congressional primaries after the Supreme Court’s Callais ruling, so all candidates appear on a single November 3 all-candidate ballot, with a December 12 runoff if nobody clears 50%.
    2026 redistricting & election structure
    Louisiana has no U.S. House nominees, and will not have any before Election Day. The Supreme Court ruled in Louisiana v. Callais on April 29, 2026 that the state’s map was an unconstitutional gerrymander. On April 30 Gov. Jeff Landry signed Executive Order 26-038 suspending the U.S. House closed party primaries set for May 16 and the June 27 runoff; the Senate primary proceeded. House races stayed on the ballot during early voting but those votes were voided and are not counted. The Legislature then passed a new map dismantling one of the state’s two majority-Black districts, likely flipping a Democratic-held seat. Under the replacement schedule the U.S. House primary is a jungle primary held Nov. 3, 2026 — the same day as the general election elsewhere — with runoffs Dec. 12, 2026. So Louisiana seats will not be decided on election night, and any candidate here is a primary entrant, not a party nominee. Several lawsuits contest the suspension. Sources: Office of the Governor of Louisiana, FEC, NBC News, Axios New Orleans.

    Michael Echols
    Louisiana · 5th District
    Jungle primary Nov 3
    Biography
    Republican candidate in Louisiana’s 5th District, in a NINE-CANDIDATE field — the largest in the state. NO NOMINEE EXISTS: all nine appear on the November 3 all-candidate ballot, with a December 12 runoff if nobody clears 50%. Born Michael Charles Echols on February 11, 1977 in Bastrop, Louisiana; lives in Monroe. BS IN ACCOUNTING, 1999, and MBA, 2001, both from the UNIVERSITY OF LOUISIANA AT MONROE. No military service. He began in banking, was chief operations officer of Oglesby Financial Group 2000-2007, then associate vice president of marketing and communication at ULM 2007-2010, before moving into development and real estate; he is a contractor and developer whose work includes renovations in downtown Monroe, and he hosts a conservative radio talk show. He served on the MONROE CITY COUNCIL 2016-2020, including as council chair, after an unsuccessful 2011 run for the state House, and has represented the 14th district in the LOUISIANA HOUSE since January 2020, sitting on Health and Welfare, Ways and Means and the joint budget panels. HE BECAME MAJORITY LEADER OF THE LOUISIANA HOUSE ON DECEMBER 11, 2025, succeeding Mark Wright. NOTE ON LOUISIANA’S ELECTION STRUCTURE, WHICH IS UNSETTLED: Act 1 of the 2024 First Extraordinary Session moved U.S. House races to closed party primaries beginning in 2026. But on APRIL 29, 2026 THE U.S. SUPREME COURT HELD IN LOUISIANA v. CALLAIS that the state’s congressional map was an unconstitutional gerrymander, and Governor Jeff Landry SUSPENDED those primaries by executive order. The Legislature approved a new map in late May with litigation looming, and Senate President Cameron Henry said that if the primaries stayed suspended the state would revert to the old all-candidate jungle system — which is what happened. That is the working basis for every Louisiana card in this file; it rests on a map passed under litigation, so VERIFY BEFORE RELYING ON A DATE.

    Ronald Russell
    Maine · 1st District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Maine’s 1st District, challenging Democratic Rep. Chellie Pingree in a rematch — his SECOND consecutive general election against her. He won the June 9, 2026 primary with 53% over Joshua Pietrowicz. No elected office held, but he has RUN THREE TIMES BEFORE: an unsuccessful bid for MAINE HOUSE DISTRICT 134, the 2022 Republican nomination for this seat, and the 2024 general, when he lost to Pingree 58.7% to 36.4%. Aged 71, RAISED IN FORT FAIRFIELD and now of KENNEBUNKPORT; his formal education is not published. HE HAD A THIRTY-YEAR CAREER IN THE UNITED STATES ARMY, SERVING AS A GREEN BERET, before retiring in the early 2000s, then FOUNDED FAR RIDGELINE ENGAGEMENTS, a North Carolina-based defense company that contracted with the Department of Defense, and SOLD IT IN 2022. On policy he opposes continuing the enhanced health insurance tax credits and wants the health system “privatized more than it is right now”; asked about a war powers resolution he said he could not say how he would vote but WOULD HAVE SUPPORTED AN AUTHORIZATION FOR THE USE OF FORCE IF PRESIDENT TRUMP HAD ASKED FOR ONE. He promises town halls “so I can hear what they think I need to be doing in Washington.” THE STREAK AT STAKE: a Republican win here would BREAK A THIRTY-YEAR RUN OF DEMOCRATS representing southern Maine. Note the geography from 2024 — Russell CARRIED inland towns such as Acton at 57.4% and Albion at 61.6% while losing the district by 22 points; the coast decides it. Pingree, seeking a TENTH term, was an ORGANIC FARMER ON NORTH HAVEN ISLAND who served as tax collector and on the school board there before the Maine Senate. Maine uses RANKED-CHOICE VOTING for congressional races.
