    Not currently serving in Congress.
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Massachusetts’s 3rd District, of ACTON, confirmed uncontested in the September 1, 2026 primary and endorsed by the Massachusetts Republican Party. HE IS A 29-YEAR U.S. ARMY VETERAN WHO RETIRED AS A COLONEL, and an IRAQ WAR veteran. HIS CIVILIAN CAREER IS IN VETERANS’ MENTAL HEALTH: a VA PSYCHIATRIC NURSE who helped open the WEST PALM BEACH VA MEDICAL CENTER from 1995 to 2000, ONBOARDING SOME 2,000 STAFF, then worked in outpatient substance abuse and psychiatry at the BEDFORD VA HOSPITAL from 2000 to 2022. HE GREW UP IN CAMBRIDGE PUBLIC HOUSING AND REGISTERED REPUBLICAN AT 18. His formal education is not published. He was also a 2024 candidate for the state legislature. He launched this campaign in March 2026 pledging to address the MERRIMACK VALLEY’S OPIOID CRISIS, and runs on affordable living, safer communities, government accountability and support for law enforcement. Unenrolled candidate Kevin Ades is also on the November ballot. NO REPUBLICAN HAS HELD MA-3 IN OVER TWO DECADES, and REPUBLICANS DID NOT FIELD A CANDIDATE HERE AT ALL IN 2024, so his candidacy restores a contest that did not exist last cycle. Rep. LORI TRAHAN, seeking a fifth term, co-chairs the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee under Hakeem Jeffries and succeeded Niki Tsongas in 2019; she faces her first primary, against Gaige Clark, after being re-elected unopposed with 97.5% in 2024 and beating Dean Tran 63.6-36.4 in 2022.
    Thomas Stalcup
    Massachusetts · 4th District
    Committee Assignments
    Not currently serving in Congress.
    Biography
    Thomas Stalcup of Brookline is the Republican nominee in Massachusetts’s 4th District, confirmed uncontested in the September 1, 2026 primary. He faces Rep. Jake Auchincloss, who has held the seat since 2021 and defeated AI researcher Jason Poulos in his own primary; independents Steve Chasse and Matthew Cook are also on the November ballot. The district runs from Newton and Brookline south through Attleboro to Fall River. No prior elected office. A Massachusetts native with a PhD in physics from Florida State University. No military service. A physicist and entrepreneur who owns a business designing software for remote weather stations. He is best known for nearly three decades of work on the 1996 crash of TWA Flight 800, which he began as a graduate student: he co-founded the Flight 800 Independent Researchers Organization, co-produced a 2013 documentary on the crash, and has pursued Freedom of Information Act litigation in Massachusetts federal court against the Missile Defense Agency, the Department of Defense and the Navy. He rejects the National Transportation Safety Board’s conclusion that a center wing fuel tank explosion brought the aircraft down, arguing instead that an errant U.S. missile was responsible; the NTSB finding remains the official determination. He describes himself as an advocate for accountability who helped organize whistleblowers exposing government misconduct. A former liberal Democrat and Bernie Sanders supporter who switched parties, he campaigns on lowering prescription drug prices and reducing U.S. military intervention abroad.
    Micah Quinney Jones
    Massachusetts · 6th District
    Committee Assignments
    Not currently serving in Congress.
    Biography
    Micah Quinney Jones of Essex is the Republican nominee in Massachusetts’s 6th District, confirmed in the September 1, 2026 primary. A securities attorney and U.S. Army veteran from Essex who served with the 82nd Airborne Division, deployed to Kabul and left the service as a captain in 2016; awarded a Bronze Star for his service in Afghanistan. He left a law practice at Morgan Lewis to run. Campaigns on a ban on congressional stock trading as his day-one measure, opening underused federal land for expedited housing, expanding energy supply including nuclear power, and national security including competitiveness in artificial intelligence. He faces Democrat Dan Koh for the seat Rep. Seth Moulton is vacating. MA-6 is the only Massachusetts seat changing hands this cycle: Seth Moulton vacated it to challenge Sen. Ed Markey, and seven Democrats are contesting the nomination. Born in Monterey, California, where his father was stationed as an active-duty Army officer, and raised in what he describes as a bipartisan household — his mother a Democrat and college librarian, his father a Republican who served 25 years with the Los Angeles Police Department after leaving the Army. He served over five years as a Military Intelligence branch detail infantry officer, deploying to Kabul with the 82nd Airborne Division, where he was intelligence adviser to the Afghan Ground Forces Command and military aide and security officer to the brigadier general leading NATO’s Rule of Law mission; he completed more than 170 missions outside the wire and was awarded the Bronze Star Medal for Meritorious Service, leaving as a captain in July 2016. He then used the GI Bill and Yellow Ribbon Program to attend Northeastern University School of Law, where he was a 2017 Rappaport Fellow in Law and Public Policy and a judicial intern to a United States federal magistrate judge in the District of Massachusetts. He practiced securities law in the Boston office of Morgan Lewis before leaving the firm to run, and lives in Essex. His stated day-one measure is a ban on congressional stock trading, alongside accountability for members of Congress, economic opportunity for the North Shore and Merrimack Valley, and national security. His opponent, Dan Koh, is a former adviser to President Biden and former chief of staff to Boston Mayor Marty Walsh who led the field in fundraising.
    Robert Gerald Burke

    Biography
    Robert Gerald Burke is the Republican nominee in Massachusetts’s 8th District, winning the September 1, 2026 primary by a wide margin over two other Republicans. He was also the party’s nominee in 2022, taking 30% against Rep. Stephen Lynch. Attended the College of the Holy Cross and served as a federal probation officer. A videographer and retired cleaning contractor, he was born in Boston and raised in Milton, and describes himself as an amateur journalist and videographer who started a videography service. This is his third consecutive run for the seat: he won the Republican primary in 2022 over Hamilton Soares Rodrigues and in 2024 over James Govatsos and Daniel Kelly, losing the general election to Rep. Stephen Lynch both times. FEC records showed him raising no money in the 2024 cycle. He faces Lynch again, who is seeking a 12th term and who first won the seat in 2001. MA-8 is rated D+15 and has elected a Democrat continuously since 1972.
    R. Tyler MacAllister
    Massachusetts · 9th District

    Biography
    Republican nominee for Massachusetts’s 9th District, confirmed by the September 1, 2026 primary. A LIFELONG CAPE CODDER, born and raised on the South Coast, who settled in MATTAPOISETT with his wife Cindy in 2001. A well-known CHARTER FISHING BOAT CAPTAIN with more than forty years on these waters, and a sales manager. His formal education is not published and no military service is listed. HE SERVED MORE THAN TWENTY YEARS IN MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENT, including FIVE TERMS ON THE MATTAPOISETT SELECT BOARD, and stepped down from that seat in April 2026 to run. He announced in June 2025 at a Marion Republican Town Committee meeting, saying he had met with White House staff in Washington and calling the race “a very winnable race based upon what happened in 2024.” HE HAS CAMPAIGNED HEAVILY ON OFFSHORE WIND: in August he ran twenty-five miles south of Nantucket to film the Vineyard Wind turbines, arguing the marine life he expected is not there. He also runs on tax cuts, school choice and constituent responsiveness, promising that people who contact the office will hear back. The district covers 49 towns across the Cape and Islands, South Coast and South Shore up to Cohasset; AT D+6 IT IS THE LEAST DEMOCRATIC DISTRICT IN MASSACHUSETTS, a state with an all-Democratic delegation, and Keating beat Dan Sullivan 56.4-43.4 in 2024. Rep. BILL KEATING, seeking a NINTH term, was Norfolk County District Attorney for twelve years and spent twenty-two years in the Massachusetts Legislature before Congress; he moved to Bourne and switched to this district in 2012 after redistricting drew his Quincy home into Stephen Lynch’s seat.

    Paul LePage
    Maine · 2nd District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Maine’s 2nd District, having won the June 9, 2026 primary. He is the former Governor of Maine, serving two terms from 2011 to 2019 before term limits ended his tenure, and he ran again in 2022, losing to Governor Janet Mills. Earlier he served on the Waterville City Council and as Mayor of Waterville from 2004 to 2011. Born in Lewiston in 1948, the eldest of eighteen children in a French-speaking household; he left home at eleven to escape an abusive father and lived on the streets before being taken in by local families. BS in business administration, Husson College; MBA, University of Maine. No military service. Spent his career in business, most prominently as general manager of Marden’s Surplus and Salvage, the Maine discount chain, and has campaigned on that record, arguing Washington needs “more real-world business experience, those who know how to create jobs.” As governor he pursued tax and welfare cuts and paid down the state’s hospital debt, and was known for a combative style and for statements that drew national criticism, including remarks about out-of-state drug dealers and about race; he described himself as “Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular” and endorsed him in 2016. In 2018 he was sued for refusing to implement voter-approved Medicaid expansion, and he added the words “stolen election” beside his signature when certifying Bruce Poliquin’s ranked-choice loss to Jared Golden. He moved to Florida after leaving office and later re-established residence in Maine, registering to vote in Augusta in 2025. Reported closing on $1 million raised, almost all from within Maine, and expects to raise $5 million. The seat is one of the most watched in the country: Golden held it four times while the district backed President Trump three times, and it is open now that Golden is not seeking re-election. Maine decides congressional general elections by ranked-choice voting. RACE STATUS, ONE SOURCE, ONE DATE: 270toWin’s mirror of the COOK POLITICAL REPORT ratings, current as of AUGUST 25, 2026, lists this district among the MOST COMPETITIVE 2026 RACES (a category that includes seats favored to flip). Cards in this file that carry no rating are NOT thereby safe — see the ledger note on the ratings pass.

    • AppropriationsAgriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies (Chairman) · Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies
    Biography
    Incumbent representing Maryland’s 1st District since January 2011, defeating Democrat Frank Kratovil in a rematch after losing to him in 2008; now in his eighth term and, since 2013, the only Republican in Maryland’s congressional delegation. Previously served in the Maryland Senate (1999–2011), winning the seat by beating an incumbent in the Republican primary and rising to Minority Whip, while continuing to practice medicine. Graduated Regis High School, New York, 1974; BS, Johns Hopkins University, 1977; MD, Johns Hopkins, 1980; MHS, Johns Hopkins, 1995. Served in the U.S. Navy Reserve Medical Corps from 1988, answering a recruitment call for anesthesiologists, and established and commanded the Johns Hopkins Medical Naval Reserve Unit; his unit was called to active duty in 1990 for Operation Desert Shield and later Desert Storm, caring for active-duty personnel, veterans and returning prisoners of war at Bethesda Naval Hospital. Retired as a commander after roughly seventeen years. An anesthesiologist at Johns Hopkins Hospital for nearly three decades, specializing in obstetric anesthesiology, where he was chief of that division and an associate professor of anesthesiology and critical care medicine. Chairman of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration and Related Agencies; also serves on its Labor-HHS-Education Subcommittee. Elected Chairman of the House Freedom Caucus on September 17, 2024, succeeding Bob Good; an original member of the caucus and a member of its board. The son of immigrants who fled communist Eastern Europe after the Second World War — his father a Hungarian anesthesiologist, his mother Polish — he was born in Brooklyn and worked nights as a blood bank technician while at Hopkins. Lives in Dorchester County.

    Biography
    Republican nominee in Maryland’s 3rd District, challenging freshman Democratic Rep. Sarah Elfreth; he won the June 23, 2026 primary. Bernard “Berney” Flowers has run before, in the 2nd District in 2022 and the 3rd in 2024. Appointed by Governor Larry Hogan in 2021 to the District 9 Judicial Nominating Commission in Howard County, and a member of the Howard County Republican Central Committee. Born in Lumberton, North Carolina. BA, University of North Carolina at Pembroke, 1987; master’s degree, Golden Gate University, 1991; graduated the United States Air Force War College, 2006; he also lists study at Harvard. Served nearly 21 years on active duty in the United States Air Force (1987–2008), retiring as a lieutenant colonel; a logistician who deployed to Iraq, Afghanistan and Ukraine and worked in 22 countries and 43 states, he was assigned to the Air Staff at the Pentagon on September 11, 2001. Authored the book Black Values Matter in 2022, hosts the weekly Loyal Opposition podcast, and serves as national political director and Maryland chapter president of Veterans for America First. Sits on the external advisory board of his alma mater. Campaigns on the national debt, federal spending, term limits and education reform. A member of Disabled American Veterans, the VFW and the American Legion, and of Phi Beta Sigma. Married more than 36 years, with two adult children and a grandchild.

    Chris Chaffee
    Maryland · 5th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Maryland’s 5th District, an open seat after Rep. Steny Hoyer, the former House Majority Leader, announced in January 2026 that he would not seek re-election after 45 years. Thirty candidates filed, among them 24 Democrats; Chaffee won the June 23, 2026 Republican primary over Michelle Talkington, who was the 2024 nominee against Hoyer and took 32%, and Bryan DuVal, who had sought the nomination in 2020 and 2022. He faces Democratic State Delegate Adrian Boafo, a 32-year-old former Hoyer staffer endorsed by Hoyer, Governor Wes Moore and Senator Angela Alsobrooks, and backed by more than $1 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s super PAC as well as tech and cryptocurrency donors. The district covers Calvert, Charles and St. Mary’s counties plus parts of Prince George’s and Anne Arundel, and forecasters rate it Safe Democratic; the last Republican to win it was Lawrence Hogan, father of the former governor, in 1972. A repeat candidate: he was the Republican nominee for the United States Senate in 2022, losing to Chris Van Hollen 65.8% to 34.1%, sought the Senate nomination again in 2024 and lost the primary to former Governor Larry Hogan, and ran for this House seat before, in 2014. He has also sought the Senate nomination in 2016 and 2018. An Upstate New York native. Graduated from the University of Maryland, College Park, in 1987. No military service. Started a small business in 1991, which he says taught him the importance of a strong economy. Describes himself as a strong conservative while saying he will work with everyone in the district; campaigns on the cost of living, economic opportunity, public safety and improving traffic for those affected by the collapse of Baltimore’s Francis Scott Key Bridge.

    Robin Ficker
    Maryland · 6th District
    Biography
    Won the June 23, 2026 Republican primary with 41.80% (16,284 votes), ahead of Chris Burnett at 37.38% and Mariela Roca at 20.83%; 214 of 214 precincts reported. Former state delegate, real estate broker and perennial candidate. Notably, Neil Parrott — the party’s nominee here in 2020, 2022 and 2024 — did not appear on the certified primary ballot. Faces Rep. April McClain Delaney, who beat former Rep. David Trone 44.0%-37.0% in a hard-fought Democratic primary. Born Robin Keith Annesley Ficker on April 5, 1943 in Takoma Park; he is 83. Attended Takoma Park Elementary and graduated from Montgomery Blair High School. Served in the United States Army from 1960 to 1966. Served ONE term in the Maryland House of Delegates, 1979 to 1983, representing Montgomery County, and has run unsuccessfully for office repeatedly since — the U.S. House six times, the U.S. Senate twice, Montgomery County Executive twice, and governor in 2022. A real estate broker and farmer, and formerly a solo-practice attorney. Nationally he is known as a Washington basketball heckler. His most durable mark is on ballot measures: he has sponsored about 25 over his career, including the 2008 Montgomery County property tax cap, and he won 1990s litigation opening Maryland court records to the public. IMPORTANT AND ON THE RECORD: Ficker was DISBARRED by Maryland’s highest court in 2022 after failing to appear at a district court trial; the court noted he had been disciplined by state and federal bars eight times for professional misconduct across his career. Hours after the Associated Press called this primary for him in June 2026 he petitioned the Maryland Supreme Court for reinstatement; as of August 2026 the Bar Counsel was OPPOSING that petition, writing that he had failed to demonstrate he understands the wrongfulness of the conduct that led to his disbarment. He campaigns as a fiscal hawk and a day-one Trump supporter, on cutting the deficit and bringing jobs to Western Maryland.

    Won the June 23, 2026 Republican primary with 43.25% (3,495 votes), ahead of Anita Mpambara Cox (26.27%), Donald Lech (17.03%) and Michael Yadeta (13.45%); 199 of 199 precincts reported. Her education, career and any military service are not published in available sources. Raskin, a prodigious fundraiser and prominent figure on Capitol Hill, easily beat three Democratic challengers in his own primary; the Montgomery County district is heavily Democratic. EDUCATION AND CAREER FOUND. BORN IN WASHINGTON, D.C. AND RAISED IN MONTGOMERY COUNTY; she took classes at MONTGOMERY COLLEGE and the UNIVERSITY OF MARYLAND, COLLEGE PARK. She is a PUBLIC RELATIONS EXECUTIVE and CEO OF CHERYL RILEY PUBLIC RELATIONS. PRIOR CANDIDACY BEYOND CONGRESS: she RAN UNSUCCESSFULLY FOR MONTGOMERY COUNTY COUNCIL IN DISTRICT 4. She was also the 2024 nominee here, beating Michael Yadeta in that primary before losing to Raskin, and she took about 69% of the 2026 Republican primary. No military service is listed. She describes herself as a “proud Christian and fearless conservative” putting America first “without apology,” campaigning on sealed borders, energy for jobs, lower costs in Maryland and PARENTS’ RIGHTS in education, and has criticized Raskin’s record on child protection and immigration. Green candidate Nancy Wallace is also on the November ballot, as she was in 2024. THE DISTRICT IS ONE OF THE WEALTHIEST AND MOST DEMOCRATIC IN THE COUNTRY: entirely within Montgomery County, D+30, with a MEDIAN HOUSEHOLD INCOME OF ABOUT $146,000. Raskin, a constitutional law professor who served in the Maryland Senate from 2007, has held the seat since 2017, took 94% of his own primary, and runs a multi-million-dollar fundraising operation drawing on national donors; he introduced legislation to form a congressional commission to assess President Trump’s fitness under the 25th Amendment, with 50 co-sponsors.

    Biography
    Incumbent representing Michigan’s 1st District since January 2017, succeeding Dan Benishek; the district covers the entire Upper Peninsula and part of the northern Lower Peninsula. No prior elected office. BA in business, Gustavus Adolphus College, 1969; MBA, University of West Florida; military education at Naval Aviation Flight Training, the Marine Corps Command and Staff College and the Combined Forces Air Component Command. Served forty years in the United States Marine Corps and Marine Corps Reserve, from 1969 to 2009, retiring as a lieutenant general — a naval aviator who flew the CH-46 and UH-1 helicopters and the T-28 and KC-130, and who served as commanding general of Marine Forces Reserve and Marine Forces North. Decorated with the Navy Distinguished Service Medal, the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, the Joint Meritorious Service Medal, the Air Medal and numerous unit awards. On his election he became the highest-ranking combat veteran ever elected to the House. Flew as a commercial pilot for Northwest Airlines for 22 years alongside his military career, and later served as president of WINGS Medical Technologies. Sits on Armed Services and Veterans’ Affairs, and on the Budget Committee, where he chairs its Oversight Task Force. A member of the Republican Study Committee and of the Great Lakes Task Force, Native American, Pro-Life, Sportsmen’s and Working Forests caucuses. Born in Shakopee, Minnesota; lives in Watersmeet with his wife Cindy, with five children and ten grandchildren.

    Terri DeBoer
    Michigan · 3rd District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Michigan’s 3rd District, challenging Democratic Rep. Hillary Scholten, who is seeking a third term. DeBoer filed on March 4, 2026 and was the FIRST Republican to enter; she won the August 4 primary over Grand Rapids attorney J. Allen Fiorletta. Her entry filled what had been a notable hole in the party’s roster: the Grand Rapids and Muskegon seat was a Republican stronghold for decades, but Scholten became the first Democrat to represent the area since the 1970s when she beat Trump’s endorsed candidate in 2022, then won by 10 points in 2024 even as Trump carried Michigan, and Republicans had dropped it from their top priorities. The district covers metro Grand Rapids and much of Kent, Ottawa and Muskegon counties. Scholten is a former social worker and immigration attorney. No elected office held; DeBoer describes herself as a political outsider, saying “West Michigan is not blue, West Michigan is not red.” Born in New Jersey and raised in a military family, which she cites in support of a strong defense; she lives in Byron Center. No military service of her own. Spent more than three decades on West Michigan television: she arrived in 1990 as a reporter at WWMT-TV in Kalamazoo, moved into meteorology in 1992, joined WOOD-TV in Grand Rapids in 1995 and forecast there for nearly thirty years before retiring in 2023, then returned to television at FOX 17 (WXMI) in 2024, leaving that role in February 2026 to run. In 1996 she earned the American Meteorological Society’s Television Seal of Approval, becoming the FIRST WOMAN in Michigan to hold the credential, and she was an on-air presence through major regional events including the 1998 derecho and the 2022 Christmas blizzard; viewers knew her as “everyone’s mom.” Campaigns on the cost of living, border security, fiscal responsibility, healthcare access and transparency, parents’ rights in medical care and education, job creation and protecting the vulnerable.

    Michael Bouchard
    Michigan · 10th District
    DCCC target
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Michigan’s 10th District, an open seat because Rep. John James left it to run for governor, making this a consequential Republican defense. He won the August 4, 2026 primary with 72.2% — 45,473 votes — over Clinton Township attorney Justin Kirk and Macomb Army veteran Steffan Demetropoulos; a fourth candidate, former Macomb assistant prosecutor Robert Lulgjuraj, withdrew after President Trump endorsed Bouchard but remained on the ballot. He faces Democrat Christina Hines, a former prosecutor in Wayne and Washtenaw counties who ran for Macomb County prosecutor in 2024. The district is centered on Macomb County with an eastern Oakland County extension, taking in Warren, Sterling Heights, Clinton Township, Shelby Township, St. Clair Shores, Roseville, Mount Clemens and Rochester Hills, and is home to roughly 800,000 people. RATING, DATED AND ATTRIBUTED: COOK POLITICAL REPORT MOVED MI-10 FROM LEAN REPUBLICAN TO TOSS-UP ON AUGUST 25, 2026. This card previously said Lean Republican, which was correct before that date and stale after it. Working Class, Green and Libertarian candidates are also on the November ballot. No prior elected office. A graduate of Michigan State University’s ROTC program. A United States Army captain who served in both the 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions and in the Michigan Army National Guard, with missions to the southern border and Iraq, and who served as chief operations officer for a 1,200-soldier infantry battalion; HE WAS AWARDED THE BRONZE STAR for his leadership on a joint task force in the global fight against ISIS, and served nearly ten years in uniform as a paratrooper; in his victory remarks he said he returned from a nine-month combat deployment to Iraq in October 2025 and began campaigning for the seat the next day. A third-generation Michigander from a family of public service: his father, Mike Bouchard, has been Oakland County Sheriff since 1999 and spent more than 38 years in law enforcement, and his grandfather served in the Army in the Second World War before working 33 years at General Motors in Warren. Campaigns on military service, manufacturing and jobs, lower costs, border security, law enforcement and parental involvement in education. NOTE: he is NOT his father — do not confuse the candidate with Sheriff Mike Bouchard, who shares the name and is not on this ballot. HE HAS RAISED HEAVILY: more than $425,000 in his first full quarter after entering the race, over $975,000 in total, with nearly $845,000 cash on hand going into the second quarter of 2026. ENDORSED BY PRESIDENT TRUMP, and also by JUDICIARY CHAIRMAN JIM JORDAN, Rep. GABE EVANS of Colorado, Rep. RYAN ZINKE of Montana, former Rep. Mike Bishop, state Senator Michael Webber and local officials across the district. Jordan called him “the America First conservative we need in Congress.” His own framing: “when I came home from Iraq, I made a commitment to keep serving… this campaign is about service, not politics.” Hines won a three-way Democratic primary with about 47% — 46,993 votes — over former Commerce Department attorney Eric Chung and former Pontiac mayor and state Rep. Tim Greimel; she was chief of the Special Victims Unit and Appeals in the Washtenaw County Prosecutor’s Office.

    Republican nominee for Michigan’s 11th District, an open Oakland County seat because Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens gave it up to run for the Senate seat Gary Peters is vacating; Stevens lost that primary to Abdul El-Sayed.     Ran unopposed in the August 4, 2026 Republican primary with 18,470 votes; NBC News called the race. Rep. Shri Thanedar lost his Democratic primary to state Rep. Donavan McKinney. The district is a Democratic stronghold and McKinney is heavily favored. Also on the November ballot: independent Maurice Gerard Morton, Libertarian Christopher James Clark and Green candidate D. Etta Wilcoxon.

Governor Tate Reeves shelved a mid-decade redistricting push that could have eliminated the district before this election. Thompson, first elected in a 1993 special election, is the lone Democrat in Mississippi’s delegation, ranking member of Homeland Security, and chaired the January 6th select committee; he was a field organizer for Fannie Lou Hamer’s 1964 congressional campaign.

    Biography
    Republican nominee for Missouri’s 5th District, challenging eleven-term Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.     Biography
    Republican nominee for Montana’s 1st District, the western seat covering Kalispell, Missoula, Butte and Bozeman. It came open when Rep. Ryan Zinke announced on March 2, 2026, days before the filing deadline, that he would not seek another term; Flint launched the same day and Zinke endorsed him. Four Republicans filed within days, turning it into the cycle’s most-watched Montana race, and Flint won the June 2 primary over Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen, the state’s top vote-getter in 2020 and 2024, former state legislator Al Olszewski, and schoolteacher Ray Curtis. Cook rates the general Likely Republican and the DCCC lists the seat among its districts in play. His first run for office. Born about 1980; a fifth-generation Montanan whose family homesteaded near Opheim and Niarada, he grew up in Glasgow and Flathead County. Graduated from the University of Montana, where he was student body president and met his wife Jessica. Enlisted after the September 11 attacks and spent more than twenty years in the Army National Guard and Army Reserve, leading combat patrols in Iraq and Afghanistan and later joining special operations units supporting counterterrorism missions in Africa and the Middle East. Worked on Greg Gianforte’s 2016 campaign for governor and served as state director for Rep. Ryan Zinke in 2016 and 2017 before deploying to Africa. Has hosted the statewide conservative talk show Montana Talks since 2009, taking leave from the program to campaign. Endorsed by President Trump, Zinke, Rep. Campaigns on land conservation, housing affordability and preserving Montana’s way of life. He faces Democrat Sam Forstag, a former smokejumper and nephew of Rep. Susie Lee of Nevada. She won the June 2, 2026 primary by just 366 VOTES — 51.4% to 48.6% over attorney Tiffany Burress, wife of former New York Giants receiver Plaxico Burress — and the Associated Press did not call it for TEN DAYS. Full name Rosemary “Rosie” Pino. PRIOR ELECTED OFFICE: SHE HAS SERVED ON THE CLIFTON CITY COUNCIL SINCE 2019, in the district’s second-largest city, and PREVIOUSLY ON THE CLIFTON SCHOOL BOARD. THE DAUGHTER OF ECUADORIAN IMMIGRANTS, a mother of eleven in a blended family, and A FORMER DEMOCRAT WHO BECAME A REPUBLICAN FOUR YEARS AGO; her campaign says she worked multiple jobs while battling cancer. Her formal education and any military service are not published. She frames her own story as proof she understands the electorate: “this isn’t about who’s the nicest or who’s the prettiest. People are entrusting you to represent them, and I am by far the most qualified because I’ve delivered.” THE DISTRICT IS THE REASON THIS RACE MATTERS: the Paterson-based, PLURALITY-HISPANIC 9th was long a Democratic stronghold — REPUBLICANS HAVE NOT WON A HOUSE ELECTION THERE SINCE THE REAGAN ADMINISTRATION — but it SHOCKINGLY VOTED FOR DONALD TRUMP IN 2024 by 49% to 48%, and the lines drawn in late 2021 made it more Republican. Two cautions recorded honestly: the primary was unusually fractious and divided the Passaic and Bergen county organizations, leaving Pino needing to unify local Republicans and raise money; and there is recent evidence of Hispanic voters shifting back toward Democrats. Also noted in coverage: in 2024 an organization she led, Latino Leaders of Clifton, endorsed a BIPARTISAN slate. Rep. Nellie Pou, unopposed in her own primary, is THE FIRST HISPANIC WOMAN TO REPRESENT NEW JERSEY IN CONGRESS; she spent decades in the state Assembly and Senate and was chosen in a hurried week-long scramble after REP. BILL PASCRELL DIED IN AUGUST 2024 at 87, having insisted on running for re-election. She has been a Republican target since taking office.     Incumbent representing New York’s 11th District since January 2021, having unseated Democratic Rep. Max Rose; the district covers Staten Island and part of southern Brooklyn and is the only Republican-held seat in New York City. Previously served a decade in the New York State Assembly (2011–2021), representing the 60th and then the 64th District, winning the seat in 2010 by defeating a two-term Democratic incumbent by ten points; she was the Republican nominee for Mayor of New York City in 2017, losing to Bill de Blasio. Graduated New Dorp High School, Staten Island, 1998, where she was class president; BA in communications, Seton Hall University, 2001, the first in her family to attend college; MBA, Wagner College, 2010. No military service. Worked as a community liaison to State Senator John Marchi (2003–2004) and to Governor George Pataki (2004–2006), then as a public affairs and government relations manager at Consolidated Edison focused on state energy policy; served as New York chair of Marco Rubio’s 2016 presidential campaign. Sits on the Ways and Means Committee. In the Assembly she worked on elder rights, keeping a Staten Island senior center open, and on repealing the MTA payroll mobility tax for small businesses, nonprofits and private schools. On her election to the Assembly she became the first Greek-American woman and the first Cuban-American woman elected to office in New York State, and the first person of Hispanic descent elected from Staten Island. Born in Manhattan and a lifelong Staten Island resident.

    Caroline Shinkle
    New York · 12th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for New York’s 12th District, an open Manhattan seat because Rep. Jerry Nadler is retiring after more than three decades, having first been elected in 1992. The redrawn district takes in the Upper West Side, the Upper East Side and all of Midtown; at D+33 it is the most Democratic district in New York and among the most lopsided in the country. She faces Democratic Assemblyman Micah Lasher, who won a crowded June primary with Nadler’s endorsement over a field that included Alex Bores, George Conway and Jack Schlossberg, a grandson of President Kennedy. The Manhattan Republican Party endorsed her on February 23, 2026, and the State Conservative Party chairman and Bruce Blakeman, the party’s candidate for governor, have also backed her. Born about 1993; her first run for public office. No military service. Graduated from MIT with a degree in economics, including a semester at Sciences Po in Paris taking all her classes in French, and earned her JD from Harvard Law School. Interned or worked at the European Central Bank in Frankfurt, the Bank of Israel in Jerusalem, where she lived for a time, and the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, before beginning her career at the Federal Reserve Board of Governors in Washington. For the past five years a corporate attorney at Cravath, Swaine and Moore in New York, handling mergers and acquisitions, capital markets and financial regulatory work; she is admitted to the bars of the United States Supreme Court, New York, Washington D.C., Ohio and Massachusetts. Campaigns on eliminating the federal income tax on W-2 wages, a balanced budget amendment and reducing the size of government, along with public safety, housing affordability and education. Her campaign is also distinguished by an emphatically pro-Israel message: she pledges to strengthen the U.S.-Israel alliance, opposes conditioning security assistance, and has criticized Nadler for missing a vote on military aid. She has said New York “is the center of global capitalism” and must not “become the center of global socialism.”

    Republican nominee for New York’s 15th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres. He was uncontested in the June 23, 2026 Republican primary. HE WON THIS SEAT IN 2022 BY DEFEATING SEAN PATRICK MALONEY, THEN CHAIRMAN OF THE DCCC — the first Republican to beat a sitting DCCC chairman in more than forty years — and held it in 2024 by six points over former Rep. Mondaire Jones. He DECLINED A 2026 RUN FOR GOVERNOR, telling the New York Times in February 2026 he would seek a third House term instead, while calling Kathy Hochul “the worst governor in America.” Born Michael Vincent Lawler on September 9, 1986 in Suffern; a lifelong Rockland County resident. THE DISTRICT HAS NEARLY 80,000 MORE REGISTERED DEMOCRATS THAN REPUBLICANS, yet swung from Biden +2 in 2020 to Trump +2 in 2024; it covers all of Rockland and Putnam plus parts of northern Westchester and southern Dutchess.     Peter Oberacker
    New York · 19th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for New York’s 19th District, challenging first-term Democratic Rep. Josh Riley in one of the most competitive races in the country. He won the June 23, 2026 primary with 77.5% over political newcomer and timber farm owner Alex Portelli on 22%, with the Associated Press calling it that night. The district sprawls from Rensselaer and Columbia counties east to Tompkins, taking in the Finger Lakes, Southern Tier, Mohawk Valley, Capital Region and Catskills, and the cities of Binghamton and Ithaca. Cook rates it Lean Democratic and the NRCC is targeting it: Riley beat Republican Marc Molinaro by fewer than 4,000 votes in 2024, taking 51.1%. Born Peter Karl Oberacker Jr. on May 13, 1963 in Merrick, New York. BA, State University of New York at Delhi. No military service. Built his private-sector career in the food industry as a RESEARCH CHEF AND FOOD SCIENTIST, helping businesses formulate new products. In office he has climbed steadily: two terms as supervisor of the Town of Maryland, then Otsego County legislator, then the New York State Senate for the 51st District since January 2021 — encouraged to run by retiring Senator James Seward and winning with 55.4% — now in his third term, covering Delaware, Schoharie, Sullivan and Otsego counties plus parts of Broome, Chenango and Ulster. He is ranking member on the Senate committees for transportation and for alcoholism and substance use disorders, and has pushed a “utility ratepayer bill of rights” requiring transparency from utilities. Endorsed by President Trump and backed by Rep. Mike Lawler, who called a candidate of his caliber critical to winning the seat back; he has raised just under $1 million. He campaigns on affordability, saying he is running so his grandchildren can live in an affordable country, and on his range of experience — “there really are two things you should never see being made: laws and sausage. And I do know both.” Riley’s campaign has attacked him as a “corporate executive for a Big Ag monopoly that put small family farms out of business.” Note for the record: Bobby Walker, who was set to become his campaign manager, was implicated in the Young Republican group chat leaks. Married to Shannon since 1986, with two children.

    New York · 20th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for New York’s 20th District, challenging nine-term Democratic Rep. Paul Tonko in the Capital Region. He announced in January 2026 and launched formally on January 23 at the Green House Social Club of La Serre in Albany, running unopposed for the nomination. The seat is safely Democratic: Tonko won 61% against Republican Kevin Waltz in 2024 and had beaten Schenectady County GOP chair Liz Joy in 2020 and 2022. Aged 75. Born in Hudson and raised in Chatham, Columbia County; he has lived in Delmar, in the town of Bethlehem, for over forty years. Served in the UNITED STATES NAVY. A career in law and law enforcement: a New York State Trooper in his youth, then Assistant Attorney General in Greene and Columbia counties from 1989 to 1996 and again under Attorney General Dennis Vacco in 1998–99, then ELEVEN YEARS as assistant counsel to the New York State Police from 1999 to 2010 — representing the same agency he had served as a trooper — followed by private practice. Now semi-retired. No prior elected office; he lost a 2010 bid for Bethlehem town justice and lost the 2024 race for Albany County District Attorney to Democrat Lee Kindlon. Campaigns on five priorities: lowering the cost of living, restoring public safety and securing the border, protecting quality of life and natural resources, government accountability, and challenging the establishment. His central attack is on energy costs — he notes he drives an electric vehicle and has solar panels, but argues Tonko’s climate votes have driven up utility bills, saying upstate is “almost the definition of unaffordability.” He questioned Tonko directly at a February town hall in Ballston Spa, and has criticized Tonko for saying he “secured” $14 million in district projects that came from an appropriations bill he voted against. Tonko, 76, has held this seat since 2013 and represented the 21st District from 2009; he is known for energy and environmental work and voted for the Inflation Reduction Act.

    Biography
    Republican nominee for New York’s 21st District, an open North Country seat after Rep. Elise Stefanik retired following a short-lived run for governor. He won the June 23, 2026 primary with about 59% to 40% over State Assemblyman Robert Smullen, who had the backing of county party leaders; Smullen remains on the November ballot on the Conservative Party line. Stefanik stayed out of the primary and congratulated Constantino afterward. The district takes in most of the North Country, the Adirondacks and the Thousand Islands, plus parts of the Mohawk Valley and greater Capital Region. His first run for office, though not his first attempt: he sought the party’s nod in late 2024 when Stefanik was nominated as U.N. Ambassador and a special election looked likely, pledging to self-fund $2.6 million, and said he would primary whoever the county chairs chose if it was not him; Trump later withdrew the nomination and Stefanik stayed. Born about 1982. No military service. Chief executive of Sticker Mule, the Amsterdam-based custom printing company he built and which serves customers worldwide; he has said he handled all of the company’s customer service himself in its early days, and argues Congress lacks a “tech mindset.” He also spent time as a professional boxer and still trains, recently with UFC champion Henry Cejudo. He became locally known in 2024 for installing a 100-foot illuminated “Vote for Trump” sign on the roof of his building in Amsterdam; the city called it a traffic hazard and sought to have it covered, a restraining order was lifted, and supporters rallied at the site. President Trump endorsed him, and the political operative Roger Stone encouraged him to run and urged the endorsement. Campaigns on bringing manufacturing and economic development to the region, expanding cell and internet service across a largely rural district, and agriculture, which he ties to the Make America Healthy Again movement.

    Kailee Buller
    New York · 22nd District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for New York’s 22nd District, challenging freshman Democratic Rep. John Mannion. She announced on March 5, 2026 and is the only Republican and Conservative candidate to qualify for the ballot, advancing directly to the general election; Republicans had struggled to field a candidate after Assemblyman John Lemondes, former Assemblyman John Salka and combat veteran David Hollenbeck all entered and then dropped out. She had the backing of every Republican and Conservative Party county chair in the district. The seat covers Onondaga and Madison counties and parts of Oneida, Cortland and Cayuga, including Syracuse, Auburn, Cortland and Utica, and has historically leaned Republican with competitive races; Cook currently rates it Solid Democratic. Her campaign argues it is a true swing district decided by independents, citing more than 154,000 Republicans and over 150,000 unaffiliated voters against a slight Democratic enrollment edge. One month into the race she reported raising $200,000 and collecting more than 7,500 Republican and over 900 Conservative petition signatures, though Mannion holds a substantial financial advantage. Her first run for office. Born about March 1989, an Auburn native. Bachelor’s degree in political science, University of Buffalo, 2011; she moved to Washington shortly afterward to work at a nonprofit. No military service. A food and economic policy advocate: chief of staff to Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins in the second Trump administration, from which she resigned to run, and chief of staff to the Deputy Secretary of Agriculture in the first; between those posts she was president and chief executive of the National Oilseed Processors Association and the Edible Oil Producers Association. Describes herself as a moderate Republican and fiscal conservative focused on utility costs, food prices and housing availability, and has said that while she has voted for President Trump she does not always agree with all his policies. Signed a no-tax-hike pledge; supports childcare tax credits, expanded health savings accounts, price transparency, faster generic drug approvals, repealing New York’s climate mandates, and a comprehensive immigration reform package, having worked on H-2A farm labor for over a decade. She and her husband Eric have three young children.

    Biography
    Incumbent representing New York’s 24th District since 2023, and in the House across three separate stints: the old 22nd District from 2017 to 2019, again from February 2021, and the 24th since redistricting. Her electoral record is unusually broken: she challenged incumbent Rep. Richard Hanna in the 2014 Republican primary and lost, won the open seat in 2016, lost it to Anthony Brindisi in 2018, and regained it in 2020 after a recount that was not certified until February 2021. Previously served in the New York State Assembly (2011–2016) for the 115th and then the 101st District, and before that as chief of staff and legal counsel to her predecessor, Assemblyman David Townsend (2003–2009). Graduated New Hartford High School, 1979; BA in political science, Colgate University, 1983; JD, Taft College of Law at the University of Cincinnati, 1987. No military service; her son Trey is a 2013 Naval Academy graduate serving as a captain in the Marine Corps. Admitted to the bar in New York, Connecticut and Florida and to all federal courts including the Supreme Court. Co-owner and legal counsel of Mid-York Press, the commercial printing and manufacturing firm her maternal grandfather founded in 1946, which employs some 80 people; a partner at Groben, Gilroy, Oster and Saunders before opening her own practice in Clinton; and founder in 1997 of Tenney Media Group, whose weekly papers reached more than 100,000 households across three counties before their sale to Gannett in 2004. Early in her career she was the only American employed by the Consulate General of Yugoslavia, which led to long ties with Utica’s Bosnian refugee community, and she published the city’s first Bosnian newspaper. Sits on Science, Space and Technology. Daughter of the late John R. Tenney, a Justice of the New York Supreme Court from 1969 to 2003; raised her son as a single mother while running the family business.

    Incumbent representing North Carolina’s 3rd District since September 2019, elected in a special election to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Rep. Walter B. Jones Jr. Previously served in the North Carolina House of Representatives (2015–2019), where in his second term he was Senior Chair of Health Policy and Chair of Health and Human Services Appropriations. Valedictorian of Broughton High School, Raleigh, a Morehead Scholar finalist who received a vice presidential appointment to the United States Naval Academy but chose medicine instead; BS, Davidson College, 1985, magna cum laude, on a full scholarship; MD, University of North Carolina School of Medicine, with honors and as a member of Alpha Omega Alpha; surgical residency in urology and renal transplantation, University of Kentucky. No military service. A urologist and business owner: former president of Eastern Urological Associates in Greenville, running a practice with more than fifty employees; Affiliate Professor of Surgery and Chief of the Division of Urology at the East Carolina University School of Medicine; and for three years Chief of Staff of Vidant Medical Center, a thousand-bed Level 1 trauma center serving 29 eastern North Carolina counties. One of very few members who still practice medicine, seeing patients a few days a month; he has long been described as the only actively practicing physician in Congress, though Rep. Mike Kennedy of Utah, elected in 2025, also practices. Has traveled as a medical missionary for more than 35 years, beginning at twenty with a summer at a Catholic leprosy hospital in Bihar, India, and since to Africa, Nicaragua and Haiti. Sits on Ways and Means, on its Health and Trade subcommittees, on Veterans’ Affairs and on House Administration. Co-chairs the House Republican Doctors Caucus and the Academic Medicine Caucus. In the state legislature he was primary sponsor of the STOP Act and the HOPE Act, North Carolina’s two principal opioid measures. Born in Tarrytown, New York, and raised in Raleigh; he and his wife Wendy have three children.

    Biography
    Incumbent representing North Carolina’s 10th District since January 2025. No prior elected office; ran unsuccessfully for the 14th District in 2022. Graduated the Francis Parker School; BS in nuclear engineering, United States Military Academy at West Point, 2009; completed the Basic Officer Leaders Course and Ranger School. Commissioned into the Infantry and served through to his time in the U.S. Army Special Forces, with more than eighteen months in combat. First assigned as an infantry platoon leader at Fort Wainwright, Alaska, he deployed to Afghanistan and at 23 took command of a remote air-access-only combat outpost in the Arghandab Valley, responsible for more than 350 American, Afghan and expatriate personnel and roughly $100 million in infrastructure and equipment. He then volunteered for and earned the Green Beret, returning to Afghanistan to lead a Special Forces detachment as its commander through a deteriorating security situation. Awarded two Bronze Stars. While still on active duty he and his wife Rocky started a firearms parts business out of their double-wide trailer home outside Fayetteville, which grew from their living room to a garage to a warehouse behind the house and now operates from a manufacturing facility in Western North Carolina; he owns ZRODelta, UnBrandedAR, US Optics and other firearms industry companies, and holds expertise in firearms design, manufacturing and regulatory matters. Sits on Armed Services, on its Readiness, Military Personnel and Intelligence and Special Operations subcommittees, and on Science, Space and Technology. Appointed in January 2025 by Chairman Mike Rogers to the West Point Board of Visitors. Born on the west coast and raised between San Diego and small-town Wyoming; the fall of Afghanistan prompted his decision to run.

    Biography
    Republican nominee for North Carolina’s 11th District, covering fifteen and a half counties of western North Carolina — an area larger than Rhode Island. SHE DID NOT WIN A PRIMARY: she was selected UNANIMOUSLY by the district’s Republican Executive Committee in August 2026 from six candidates, after Rep. CHUCK EDWARDS ENDED HIS RE-ELECTION CAMPAIGN FOLLOWING AN ETHICS COMMITTEE INVESTIGATION alleging sexual harassment and a toxic work environment; he had trailed Democrat Jamie Ager three to one in fundraising. She took the nomination with 82 DAYS to build a campaign that would normally take a year, and her move triggered a second executive-committee process to replace her on the state House ballot. Born in Henderson County in 1978 or 1979 and has lived there her whole life, growing up on the family farm; she says her family has called Western North Carolina home for EIGHT GENERATIONS. Graduated East Henderson High School and earned an ASSOCIATE DEGREE IN BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION FROM BLUE RIDGE COMMUNITY COLLEGE in 2016. No military service. MORE THAN TWENTY YEARS IN MORTGAGE BANKING as a small business owner and mortgage loan officer, currently with ALCOVA. She has served in the NORTH CAROLINA HOUSE for District 117 since 2022, re-elected in 2024, where she CHAIRS THE INSURANCE COMMITTEE and the Appropriations Committee on Agriculture, Natural and Economic Resources, and is VICE CHAIR OF FULL APPROPRIATIONS and of the HOUSE SELECT COMMITTEE ON HELENE RECOVERY. Before the legislature she was vice president of the Hendersonville Women’s Club, treasurer of the Mortgage Bankers Association of Western North Carolina, and on the boards of the Henderson County Education Foundation, AdventHealth Foundation, the county Planning Board and St. Gerard House, a non-profit serving people affected by autism. HER PARTY REGISTRATION HAS CHANGED OVER TIME: Libertarian 2002-2005, Democratic 2005-2016, Republican since 2016. Her campaign centers on affordability, community safety, farmers and continued recovery from HURRICANE HELENE, which devastated the region in 2024. Her opponent is JAMIE AGER, a fourth-generation farmer. Western Carolina University’s Chris Cooper has said that despite entering late she has a good shot at the seat. RACE STATUS, ONE SOURCE, ONE DATE: 270toWin’s mirror of the COOK POLITICAL REPORT ratings, current as of AUGUST 25, 2026, lists this district among the MOST COMPETITIVE 2026 RACES (a category that includes seats favored to flip).     Biography
    Republican nominee for North Carolina’s 12th District, advancing from the March 3, 2026 primary. No prior elected office. Graduated Scotts Valley High School, California; BS in finance, Leavey School of Business, Santa Clara University. No military service. Works as a finance professional. Campaigns on a conservative platform including opposition to elective abortion. Little further public record is available. He won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary over Addul Ali, who chairs the Cabarrus County GOP and the 12th District GOP and was the party’s 2024 nominee here. His first political race. A FINANCE PROFESSIONAL. His formal education and any military service are not published in available sources. HIS PLATFORM IS UNUSUAL AND WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANY CONVERSATION: alongside equal justice under the law and free-market economics, he calls for ABOLISHING THE FEDERAL RESERVE AND RETURNING TO GOLD AND SILVER. He says he ran because of “a calling on my heart from God” and frames the race around debt and housing, citing $40 trillion in national debt and a first-time home buyer average age of 40, and noting that 51% of Charlotteans are housing burdened. He credits Rep. Alma Adams with naming the affordability problem correctly but argues she is subsidizing it rather than fixing root causes: “you can’t central plan prosperity.” Adams, for context, has held the Charlotte seat since a 2014 special election succeeding Melvin Watt, spent TWENTY YEARS in the North Carolina House before that, and is the LONGEST-SERVING DEMOCRAT in North Carolina’s delegation; she founded the Congressional Bipartisan HBCU Caucus and co-founded the Black Maternal Health Caucus, holds a PhD from Ohio State and taught art at Bennett College, and her district has been reconfigured four times in her ten years in Congress. She won 62.7% in 2022 and beat Ali in 2024.

Born in Shaker Heights into a prominent Cleveland family: his grandfather Sam Miller was co-chair emeritus of Forest City Realty Trust, his grandmother Ruth ran for Congress in 1980, his father Abe owns a cap manufacturing company in Cleveland, and his uncle Aaron David Miller is a Middle East scholar. Lives in Bay Village.     Patti Adair
    Oregon · 5th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Oregon’s 5th District, challenging first-term Democratic Rep. Janelle Bynum; she won the May 19, 2026 primary with about 57% over Jonathan Lockwood, a former legislative spokesman, and the Associated Press called it the same evening. The district is Oregon’s most competitive, running from the southeastern Portland suburbs across parts of the Willamette Valley and over the Cascades to Bend; it has more nonaffiliated voters than either party but more registered Democrats than Republicans, and Cook rates it Likely Democratic. It was held by one-term Republican Lori Chavez-DeRemer before Bynum won in 2024. Adair had raised more than $300,000 to Bynum’s $365,000 this year, with Bynum holding more than $2.2 million on hand. Has served on the Deschutes County Commission since 2019 and previously led the county Republican Party; she announced for Congress in November 2025 and did not seek re-election to the commission. A delegate for President Trump at the 2016 Republican National Convention. Born about 1952. BA in history, University of Oregon; later earned her CPA in Washington State. No military service. A businesswoman and philanthropist who spent her career in California before returning to Oregon in 2014. Awarded the Master Parachutist Badge, the Ranger Tab and the Special Forces Tab, and held the highest levels of security clearance, including service at the Pentagon on waived special access programs. Later worked as a defense contractor. Sits on the Foreign Affairs and Science, Space and Technology committees. A fifth-generation Texan born in a military hospital in Philadelphia during his father’s Army service; he met his wife Tracy through a Young Life fellowship group and they have been married since his graduation from West Point, living in McKinney.

    Biography
    Republican nominee for Texas’s 9th District, a seat in east Harris County redrawn in the 2025 Texas redistricting from a Democratic-leaning district long held by Rep. Al Green into one President Trump carried 59.5% to 39.6% in 2024. She won the May 26, 2026 primary runoff with 68% against state Rep. Afterward moved to Houston for a career in energy finance, advising on billion-dollar mergers and acquisitions, and is now a small business owner. Endorsed by the National Border Patrol Council and local police unions. A wife and mother raising her children in the district; she faces Democrat Leticia Gutierrez in November.     Texas · 10th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Texas’s 10th District, an open seat after Rep. Michael McCaul announced in September 2025 that he would not seek re-election after more than two decades. Gober won the March 3, 2026 primary outright with over 51% in a ten-candidate field, avoiding a runoff, with President Trump’s endorsement and more than $1 million raised; Ballotpedia had identified it as a battleground primary. The redrawn district runs from part of Austin across roughly 150 miles to west Houston, covering all or part of thirteen counties, with nearly a third of its population in Brazos County, home to Texas A&M; it is an R+10 seat that Trump carried 60–38 in 2024. No prior elected office. BS, Texas A&M University, class of 2001; JD, Harvard Law School. No military service. Served in national security and border security roles at the United States Department of Justice and as chief counsel to the Republican Party of Texas, then built a conservative election law practice; he founded Lex Politica and is general counsel at Maven Advocacy Partners. In 2024 he was director and chief lawyer of America PAC, the super PAC founded by Elon Musk, defending the legal challenge to its million-dollar payments to swing state voters, and he was reported to be on retainer with the Republican National Committee. He cites legal wins against former special counsel Jack Smith and against the IRS in the Lois Lerner litigation. He is also one of the few Texas Republicans publicly identified as having played a central role in the 2025 Texas redistricting, which produced the map he is now running on. A seventh-generation Texan, born and raised in rural Texas. Faces Democrat Caitlin Rourk in November.

    Texas · 16th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Texas’s 16th District, challenging four-term Democratic Rep. Veronica Escobar, who was unopposed in her own primary; the district covers most of El Paso County. He took 24% in a seven-candidate March 3, 2026 primary and won the May 26 runoff with about 69% against Manuel Barraza, a former judge convicted of wire fraud and deprivation of honest services in 2010 who served four years in prison. No Republican has won this seat since 1962, and national Republican leaders have not placed it on their target lists. His first run for office. Born about 1977 in Phoenix. Served in the United States Navy as a Special Warfare Combatant Crewman. Afterward joined the U.S. Border Patrol, serving on the Border Patrol Tactical Team, and came to El Paso when stationed there in 2001; now retired from the agency and running a canine drug detection business. Campaigns on El Paso property taxes, which he argues are inflated by school budgets and bond measures, on support for local and small business, on border security, and on veterans’ care and benefits. He has said he is running because he wants a representative not beholden to Washington insiders or special interests. He filed no campaign finance reports with the Federal Election Commission during the campaign, which is required only above a $5,000 threshold; Escobar had raised more than $730,000 by March. He declined repeated interview requests from local press and campaigned largely through social media video. Registered to vote in 2002 and had not voted in a Republican primary in El Paso before his own name appeared on the ballot in March.

    Mark Teixeira
    Texas · 21st District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Texas’s 21st District, an open Hill Country seat after Rep. Chip Roy chose to run for Texas Attorney General rather than seek re-election. He won the March 3, 2026 primary outright with about 61% in a twelve-candidate field, avoiding a runoff and finishing more than 50 points ahead of the next candidate, with endorsements from President Trump and Governor Greg Abbott; one rival ended his campaign in February and immediately endorsed him. The district covers parts of Hays and Bexar counties and all of Real, Kerr, Kendall, Gillespie, Comal, Blanco and Bandera counties, and was left largely unchanged by the 2025 redistricting; no Democrat has represented it since 1978. No prior elected office. Born in 1979. BS in business administration, Georgia Institute of Technology, which he attended as a student-athlete. No military service. A five-time Gold Glove winner and three-time All-Star at first base. Since retiring he has invested in small businesses, startups and real estate, and worked with the Texas Public Policy Foundation, supporting Governor Abbott and Rep. Roy on conservative policy and advocating for school choice. Moved back to Texas in 2021 and lives in Bee Cave in Central Texas with his wife and three children.     Brandon Herrera
    Texas · 23rd District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Texas’s 23rd District, the sprawling border seat running from San Antonio to outside El Paso. No prior elected office. He challenged Rep. Tony Gonzales in the 2024 Republican primary, forcing a runoff and losing by fewer than 400 votes, then ran again in 2026, finished first in the March 3 primary and became the nominee two days later when Gonzales withdrew after admitting an affair with a former staffer who had since died; the House Ethics Committee opened an investigation into whether Gonzales engaged in sexual misconduct toward an employee, and Speaker Mike Johnson had called on him to end the campaign. Studied pre-law at Campbell University before leaving to start a business. No military service; both his parents come from military families. Founded and runs a small firearms manufacturing company near San Antonio, and is known online as The AK Guy, hosting a firearms YouTube channel with more than three million subscribers and, by his campaign’s account, over half a billion views. A Second Amendment activist, he first ran after criticizing Gonzales’s vote for the bipartisan gun safety bill that followed the 2022 Uvalde school shooting, in a town inside the district. Campaigns on border security, tax and regulatory cuts, the REINS Act and veterans’ health care. The primary rivalry was bitter: Gonzales publicly called him a neo-Nazi, a characterization Herrera rejects, and his past videos and remarks have drawn criticism. Born in 1995 and of Hispanic heritage with Texas family roots; he moved to the San Antonio area in 2021 and is among the youngest nominees in the country. Faces Democrat Padilla Stout in November.     Biography
    Republican nominee for Texas’s 32nd District and the presumptive next congressman: the seat was redrawn in the August 2025 Texas redistricting from a compact Dallas district with a D+22 baseline into one stretching into East Texas at R+17, and Inside Elections moved it from Solid Democratic to Solid Republican. With his wife Elizabeth he co-founded Saint Francis Academy, a classical Christian school. Endorsed by President Trump, Governor Greg Abbott, and Reps. Lance Gooden and Keith Self, with support from Club for Growth and from Leading the Future, an artificial-intelligence policy PAC. A seventh-generation Texan from Rockwall raising five children.     Biography
    Republican nominee for Texas’s 34th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in one of the party’s top national pickup targets. A Rio Grande Valley native from Mission and a Spanish speaker in a district that is more than 90% Hispanic.     Republican nominee for Texas’s 35th District, a redrawn San Antonio-area seat that Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato’s Crystal Ball each rated Likely Republican as of March 2026; Inside Elections judged Democrats could take it only in a blue wave.     Riley Owen
    Utah · 1st District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Utah’s 1st District. AGED 27 — THE YOUNGEST NOMINEE IN THIS FILE. He won the nomination outright at the April 25, 2026 state convention with 71.2% OF DELEGATES, and advanced straight to the general because his rivals Dave Robinson and Stone Fonua ran as convention-only candidates and never gathered signatures. A DESCENDANT OF SIX GENERATIONS OF UTAHNS, with DEGREES FROM PRINCETON AND OXFORD in international affairs and public policy. Endorsed by Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and by Robert O’Brien, President Trump’s former national security adviser. THE DISTRICT EXISTS BECAUSE OF A COURT ORDER: in November a district judge REPLACED UTAH’S CONGRESSIONAL MAP WITH ONE OF HER OWN, turning one of four red districts blue and creating a Salt Lake County seat that KAMALA HARRIS CARRIED BY 24 POINTS. The state’s incumbents scattered — Blake Moore moved to the 2nd, Celeste Maloy to the 3rd, Mike Kennedy to the 4th, and Burgess Owens retired — leaving no Republican incumbent here. His opponent is FORMER REP. BEN McADAMS, who has $300,000 on hand to Owen’s $9,500. HIS PITCH IS UNUSUAL: he calls it “COMMUNITY CONSERVATISM” with Gen Z characteristics, argues conservatives need to learn how to talk about MATERNITY LEAVE AND THE ENVIRONMENT, and launched a “Hard Questions” tour in August. He walked onstage at the convention to Billy Joel’s “We Didn’t Start the Fire” and said he was “not willing to let progressive ideologies dissolve” the American dream “into a mere fantasy.” Utah GOP Chair Rob Axson, a critic of the court map, says there is “nothing competitive” about the new districts in a general election. Spent roughly a decade as a soil conservationist with the Natural Resources Conservation Service in Beaver, Utah, work she began through an internship secured as an undergraduate, then after law school served as a deputy county attorney for Washington County, a staff attorney for the Washington County Water Conservancy District, and public lands policy attorney for the Utah Association of Counties, before joining Stewart’s Washington office for four years. Sits on the Appropriations Committee. Raised in a single-wide trailer in the small town of Hiko, Nevada with five siblings, just across the state line; born in Cedar City. Her expertise is in public lands, water and federal land agencies — the defining issues of a district that is largely federal land.

    Gerald Malloy
    Vermont · At-Large
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Vermont’s at-large district, challenging Democratic Rep. Becca Balint, who is seeking a third term and was unopposed in her own primary, taking 98.4% against write-ins. Malloy won the August 11, 2026 Republican primary with 76.3% over perennial candidate Mark Coester; the Associated Press called it less than an hour after polls closed with about 10% counted. Vermont HAS NOT ELECTED A REPUBLICAN TO THE U.S. HOUSE SINCE 1990. This is his THIRD run for federal office: he was the Republican nominee for the United States Senate against Peter Welch in 2022 and against Bernie Sanders in 2024, losing both, and entered this race with statewide name recognition. A graduate of the United States Military Academy at West Point — he first visited as a boy for a hockey tournament and decided then that he wanted to attend — and a retired Army officer who served 22 years on active duty. Afterwards he worked for defense contractors and as a business owner; he moved to Vermont in 2020 and lives in Weathersfield. No prior elected office. He campaigns under the slogan “Deploy Malloy” on affordability, border security, energy independence and reducing government spending, and says years of progressive governance have driven costs up and people out. His distinctive pitch is a working alliance with Republican Governor Phil Scott, arguing the congressional delegation has not supported him and that he would use Washington contacts to attract private employers to a state he calls business-unfriendly. He has also said he would lower the political temperature, contrasting himself with a delegation he describes as focused on “angry rhetoric.” Notably for a Republican nominee, he has criticized President Trump on some matters while supporting the American military action in Iran. He and Coester both declined Vermont Public’s invitation to a primary debate.

    Biography
    Won the Republican primary with 56.6% over Philip Harding (30.7%) and Rick Smithers (12.8%); AP called the race 30 minutes after polls closed. Retired U.S. Army Lt. Col. who taught at West Point and served as a National Security Council director. Faces first-term Democratic Rep. Eugene Vindman in a race expected to be competitive. Note: one aggregator listed him as “Derrick” Ollivant; AP, WTOP and NBC all use Doug. REPUBLICANS BELIEVE THIS IS THEIR BEST CHANCE TO FLIP A SEAT IN VIRGINIA. He won the August 4, 2026 primary with 56.6% — 13,337 votes — over Prince William entrepreneur Philip Harding on 30.7% and pastor Rick Smithers on 12.8%, and he OUTRAISED THE FIELD at $251,134 by mid-July, almost double Harding’s total. State Senator Tara Durant had also been in the race earlier. Born August 29, 1967 in Hillsboro, Oregon; he grew up there, has lived in Virginia for ten years and in Culpeper County since 2020. Attended INDIANA UNIVERSITY, JAMES MADISON UNIVERSITY and WHEATON COLLEGE. A RETIRED UNITED STATES ARMY LIEUTENANT COLONEL with TWO COMBAT TOURS IN IRAQ who also advised coalition forces in Afghanistan, SERVED ON THE NATIONAL SECURITY COUNCIL as a director, and TAUGHT AT WEST POINT. Now managing partner of Mantid International, an international consulting firm. His first run for office. A practicing Catholic, father of seven and grandfather of two. Campaigns on a “manufacturing renaissance for Virginia” so families can afford to stay in the state, cutting federal spending, the military, border security, grid capacity, and an unusual health-and-fiscal argument: “we’re broke because we’re sick,” and fixing the food supply would reduce the deficit. He rejects the charge of district-shopping, saying he stayed put through the Democrats’ redistricting push. THE SEAT IS GENUINELY CLOSE AND NARROWING: it produced VIRGINIA’S CLOSEST HOUSE RACE IN 2024, when Vindman beat Derrick Anderson 51.18% to 48.54%, a margin of 10,489 votes; in 2022 Yesli Vega lost to Abigail Spanberger — now Governor — by 12,771. THE MATCHUP IS TWO RETIRED ARMY LIEUTENANT COLONELS: Vindman, born in Kyiv and the brother of Alexander Vindman, served 1998–2022 in the Judge Advocate General’s Corps.     Biography
    Republican nominee for Virginia’s 8th District, challenging Democratic Rep. Don Beyer in one of the most Democratic seats in the country — Arlington, Alexandria and part of Fairfax County. He filed ON THE FIRST DAY of the window and was the lone Republican to do so, running unopposed for the nomination. Full name Antony “Tony” Sabio, aged 51, born November 19, 1974 IN SAN JUAN, PUERTO RICO — THE SON OF A PUERTO RICAN MOTHER AND A FILIPINO FATHER — and raised in the harder neighborhoods of SAN DIEGO. He has lived in Virginia since 2002. He ATTENDED LIBERTY UNIVERSITY, studying SOCIOLOGY. OVER TWO DECADES OF MILITARY AND GOVERNMENT SERVICE: THE UNITED STATES NAVY, then the SECRET SERVICE, then the CIA. He then moved into the private sector and is CEO AND FOUNDER OF ROCKFINN GROUP LLC, a professional security protection company. No elected office held, but he has RUN TWICE — for the FAIRFAX COUNTY SCHOOL BOARD, and in 2023 for the PROVIDENCE DISTRICT SEAT ON THE FAIRFAX COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS, losing to incumbent Karl Frisch, who later became board president. He calls himself a REAGAN-STYLE CONSERVATIVE: “there’s two things I live by — one is my faith as a Christian, and the other one is the Constitution of the United States.” He and his wife Abigail have FIVE CHILDREN, one of them adopted. THE MONEY GAP IS ENORMOUS: Sabio had raised $21,917 to Beyer’s MORE THAN $2.1 MILLION, with $860,000 on hand as of July 1. Libertarian Shelly Arnoldi and independent Tim Sharman are also on the November ballot. Beyer, seeking a SEVENTH term, won two-thirds of a five-way Democratic primary; he CHAIRS THE JOINT ECONOMIC COMMITTEE, sits on Ways and Means and on Science, Space and Technology where he chairs the Space Subcommittee, was LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR OF VIRGINIA 1990-1998 and AMBASSADOR TO SWITZERLAND AND LIECHTENSTEIN under President Obama, and built a four-decade family car business from a 1974 summer job.

    Dave Beckwith
    Virginia · 10th District
    Biography
    Republican nominee for Virginia’s 10th District, challenging freshman Democratic Rep. Suhas Subramanyam. He won the August 4, 2026 primary decisively, taking about 72% of a four-candidate field; the Associated Press called it at 7:27 p.m., less than half an hour after polls closed. He led the Republican field in fundraising. His rivals were high school World History teacher Julie Perry and national security specialist Anthony Suttles; retired Army Lieutenant Colonel Sam Wong withdrew despite having led early fundraising. The district covers all of Loudoun County — more than half its voters — plus Fauquier and Rappahannock counties, Manassas and Manassas Park, western Prince William and part of southern Fairfax. With a median household income near $141,000 it is among the wealthiest districts in the country, and Cook rates it Solid Democratic; even so the general could be competitive, since Subramanyam beat Republican Mike Clancy by about 4.5 points in 2024. This is his SECOND run: he sought the seat in 2022 and lost that primary to Hung Cao, and this is the first primary he has won. No elected office held, though he has been active in Loudoun Republican politics. Born about 1965; lives in Sterling. Bachelor’s degree in aerospace engineering, University of Notre Dame; master’s in mechanical engineering, University of Dayton; graduate of the United States Army War College. Served 30 years in the United States Air Force, retiring in 2017 as a colonel, and rose to serve as a deputy assistant secretary of defense. Afterward worked for the government contractors Orbital ATK and SAIC. Subramanyam, elected in 2024 to succeed Jennifer Wexton, previously served in the Virginia House of Delegates and State Senate and co-founded the General Assembly’s first Asian American and Pacific Islander Caucus.

She led the August 4, 2026 top-two primary with 34.9%, ahead of Democrat John Duresky on 30.8%, with Republicans Jerrod Sessler and Matt Boehnke far behind at 14.3% and 10.3%. Duresky, a retired Air Force officer who worked at the Hanford cleanup site, is trying to become the first Democrat to win the seat since Jay Inslee in 1992. Has served on the Yakima County Board of Commissioners since 2019, first elected in 2020. She announced days after Newhouse’s retirement and led the field in fundraising early, raising $523,892 by the end of March. Endorsed by President Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, and helped by roughly $2.2 million in outside spending, most of it from super PACs backed by the cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence industries; she did not have the backing of the county Republican central committees. No military service. Spent her career in banking, a background she cites in arguing government should check for fraud the way lenders do. Campaigns as an America First Republican on border security, the Second Amendment, ending diversity, equity and inclusion programs, and government spending, and argues the district has lacked visible leadership. Her relationship with her predecessor is complicated and worth knowing: she appeared in a 2024 television advertisement endorsing Newhouse and attacking Sessler, then said at a December 2025 Turning Point USA event that she had a yearslong plan to “retire” Newhouse over his 2021 vote to impeach President Trump. Newhouse has said he will not endorse either candidate in November.

    Republican nominee for Washington’s 6th District, advancing from the August 4, 2026 top-two primary behind Democratic Rep. Emily Randall, who led with about 60%. Randall, elected in 2024, previously served in the Washington State Senate and was one of three freshman Democrats who competed for the House Democratic Caucus freshman class representative post that year. Of BREMERTON. She announced on March 6, 2026 and pitches herself to the region’s industries — “our maritime workers, timber families, fishermen, tribes, and military communities deserve a voice in Congress that understands their lives.” Her platform is public safety, taxes and economic vitality; she claims OVER THIRTY YEARS OF EXPERIENCE including regulatory compliance at federal, state and local levels, says she has WRITTEN STAKEHOLDER LEGISLATION affecting regional industries and MANAGED MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR BUDGETS, and describes herself as a consensus builder. RANDALL BECAME THE FIRST LGBTQ+ LATINA IN CONGRESS when elected in 2024 to succeed Derek Kilmer; a Wellesley graduate who majored in Spanish, she worked for Planned Parenthood and served two terms in the Washington State Senate.

    Republican nominee for Washington’s 7th District, advancing from the August 4, 2026 top-two primary with about 10.8% behind Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal on 83.3%. The Seattle-based district is rated D+39, among the most Democratic in the country.
